ef78496c13:d863335331c5f44a.title: Value-added Taxation of Hospitality Services from the Standpoint of Equal Tax Treatment and Competitive Neutrality
ef78496c13:d863335331c5f44a.author: Markkanen, Jaakko
ef78496c13:d863335331c5f44a.summary: Abstract Theoretical studies suggest that VAT should have only one rate. These results, however, rest on assumptions that do not hold for all services. In practice, the buyer can replace certain taxed services with their own untaxed household work, with tax-free sales on passenger ships or with a service taxed in another country. A meal cooked at home for oneself is outside the scope of VAT, but a meal produced in a restaurant is not. From the neutrality of taxation perspective, this provides a rationale for targeting reduced VAT rates at all services with close home-produced substitutes. A one-hour flight from Helsinki to Stockholm carries no VAT, but a one-hour flight to Oulu does. Competition would become more equal if an ad valorem tax were levied on transport for international trips starting in Finland. Shipping companies receive a crew subsidy that onshore businesses do not. From a purely economic standpoint, the VAT exemption for restaurant sales on board could on these grounds be abolished, as could the crew subsidy for catering and service staff on passenger ships. This conclusion does not take into account the security-of-supply perspective on how the changes would affect freight capacity in foreign trade and market equilibrium.

ef78496c13:1ef842bb2fe92319.title: Short-Term Incidence of Property Tax Hikes on Professionally Managed Apartments – Evidence from Philadelphia
ef78496c13:1ef842bb2fe92319.author: Sisi Zhang
ef78496c13:1ef842bb2fe92319.summary: Property tax incidence — who ultimately bears the tax burden — has long been central to public finance. In markets with imperfect competition, tax incidence may vary with market structure and strategic interactions, allowing landlords to absorb more or less of the tax burden than standard tax incidence theory would suggest. Exploiting a policy shock of a delayed comprehensive reassessment in Philadelphia and a unique property-level longitudinal rent dataset, this study revisits the issue of short-term tax incidence of property tax. We document that about 73 percent of tax increases were passed through to tenants in professionally managed large-scale apartments, with effects emerging approximately three quarters after the policy shock. However, we find no significant evidence of tax-induced rent increases at the broader market level, likely due to the smaller tax increases faced by most large multifamily properties and weaker cost pass-through among smaller rentals. This paper enriches the tax incidence literature by providing new evidence on the short-term tax pass-through and sheds light on the heterogeneity of landlord behavior, with implications for the optimal design of property tax systems.

ef78496c13:49bc024c668a9be8.title: Public Goods and Distribution under Multidimensional Heterogeneity
ef78496c13:49bc024c668a9be8.author: Johansson-Stenman, Olof
ef78496c13:49bc024c668a9be8.summary: How should distributional concerns influence applied welfare analysis and its policy recommendations? Using a variational approach, we extend the classical problem of public good provision under optimal nonlinear income taxation to allow for multidimensional heterogeneity in abilities, preferences, and exposure to public goods. We derive a general policy rule where the deviation from the Samuelson condition is governed by the difference between the cross-sectional and within-individual income elasticities of the marginal willingness to pay for the public good. This novel sufficient statistic applies regardless of the structure of unobserved heterogeneities. Particular attention is paid to exposure heterogeneity, e.g., in terms of distance to the public good, which can generate substantial deviations from the Samuelson condition. The results suggest that it is often optimal to address distributional concerns explicitly in public good provision, rather than solely through the tax and transfer system.

ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.author: Ana Popovici
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

ef78496c13:7b5646d56b367a97.title: Knowledge Without Taxation? Experimental Evidence from a Tax Education Program
ef78496c13:7b5646d56b367a97.author: Konstantin Poensgen
ef78496c13:7b5646d56b367a97.summary: A property tax experiment in Ghana randomly provides tax education to property owners and frontline officials. The intervention raises tax knowledge, which spreads through social networks to untreated neighbors, but does not increase tax payments. Educated taxpayers and officials become more engaged in their interactions without developing more collaborative relationships. Taxpayers revise downward their beliefs about enforcement capacity and become more aware of legal ways to reduce their tax burden. Knowledge is a double-edged sword: it can stimulate citizens to engage with the tax system while exposing the state's limited capacity to enforce it.

ef78496c13:01b2088d0a2ac965.title: How do Top Earners Respond to Taxation? Own- and Cross-Tax Base Responses, Efficiency, and Inequality
ef78496c13:01b2088d0a2ac965.author: Horacio Rueda
ef78496c13:01b2088d0a2ac965.summary: This paper presents new evidence on how top income earners respond to changes in the personal labor income tax schedule, uncovering both own- and cross-tax base responses within a unified framework. For identification, we exploit a 2012 tax reform in Uruguay that generated quasi-random variation in top marginal rates within the top 1% of the labor income distribution. Our empirical approach relies on a difference-in-differences identification strategy and administrative records linked at the individual level across multiple tax bases. We estimate an own-tax base intensive margin elasticity of 0.82 and extensive margin semi-elasticity of 3.36. Extensive margin responses are mostly driven by taxpayers shifting from the personal labor income tax base toward corporate income or capital income tax bases (semi-elasticities of -1.00 and -0.61, respectively). Our preferred estimates suggest that the reform was effective in increasing tax revenues, with efficiency costs representing 31% of the projected increase. However, it had limited impact on inequality, most likely due to its narrow scope and income shifting toward tax bases with lower and flat rates. Overall, our results indicate that policy efforts aiming to reduce inequality by increasing top marginal tax rates should also focus on limiting income shifting opportunities to strengthen their redistributive effects.

ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.title: The Transparency Tax : Discouraging Firm Ownership via Tax Havens
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.author: Bajaña, Alex
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.summary: Tax havens weaken tax enforcement by obscuring firm ownership and facilitating offshore evasion. This paper studies a reform in Ecuador that imposed a corporate tax surcharge on firms with owners in tax havens, using a newly available ownership registry. Comparing haven-owned firms to other foreign-owned firms, the analysis finds that the reform reduced haven ownership by 12 percentage points, largely through disclosure of non-haven individual owners. Exposed firms reduced transactions with tax havens and increased corporate tax payments, with no detectable effects on investment or firm size. The results suggest that ownership transparency can meaningfully improve tax compliance at limited efficiency cost, even through unilateral action.

ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.title: Partners on a Climb : Financial Sector Development and Tax Collections in Indonesia
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.author: Polat, Beyza
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.summary: Shallow financial markets may act as an important structural constraint on a country’s ability to mobilize tax revenues. This paper explores this hypothesis in the context of Indonesia, a middle-income country with persistently low tax collections and low financial sector depth. At the macro level, relating cross-country financial development to new estimates of tax gaps, it finds that a 1 percent increase in private credit as a share of GDP could reduce the tax gap by approximately 0.2 percent. At the micro level, analysis of publicly listed Indonesian companies suggests that a one-decile increase in financial constraints is associated with a 0.18 percentage point drop in cash effective tax rates, indicating that financially constrained firms may be using tax planning as a liquidity tool. The results suggest that tax collections are positively associated with financial sector deepening.

ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.title: Low fertility rates: A fiscal policy perspective
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.author: Baur, Martin
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.summary: Switzerland’s fertility rate fell below 1.3 children per woman in 2024 and has remained well below the replacement level for decades, reflecting a broader trend across advanced economies. This paper discusses the economic and fiscal implications of persistently low fertility, reviews its underlying causes and the extent to which family policy can influence fertility decisions, and presents policy options available for Switzerland. Low fertility slows growth of the domestic working-age population, accelerates population ageing, and reduces long-term economic growth potential. For public finances, it dampens tax revenues and social insurance contributions while increasing age-related expenditure, particularly on pensions and healthcare. The causes of low fertility are multifaceted, including the financial costs of having children, difficulties in reconciling work and family life, and broader changes in social norms and lifestyles. Evidence from OECD countries suggests that family policies can alleviate some constraints, but their effects on fertility are small and often temporary. Coherent and well-coordinated measures supporting families throughout the child-rearing years appear more promising than individual measures. As a sustained reversal of current fertility trends appears unlikely, economic and fiscal policy should focus on adapting to an ageing society by making better use of the domestic labour supply, facilitating labor-market-oriented immigration, and fostering productivity growth. Finally, reforms to strengthen the fiscal sustainability of pension and healthcare systems become even more important.

ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.title: The Fiscal Alibi: Hidden Spending Needs and Government Reputation
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.summary: A government may ask for a high tax because it faces a genuine expense. The same demand can also be made by a government that intends to keep the proceeds. We study this ambiguity in a two-period reputation model with privately observed spending needs and an endogenous tax base. The opportunist chooses between outright confiscation and levies that an honest government might impose. We characterize the three possible regimes through a single equilibrium equation. A mean-preserving spread of legitimate needs weakly raises the opportunist’s lifetime value, with a strict increase precisely when the spread changes the upper tail relevant for mimicry. We then give a necessary and sufficient curvature condition for this ordering to extend to a general reputational continuation prize. Verification reduces the value of concealment, but also changes how the opportunist extracts. In the benchmark economy, greater auditing weakly lowers current citizen welfare, even before audit costs, while improving the future allocation through better information. The welfare case for verification consequently depends on the balance between these two effects. Examples yield no auditing, an optimum within a regime, and an optimum at the boundary between regimes.

ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.title: Taxing Capital to Protect It
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.summary: This paper studies the composition of taxation when the government cannot fully commit to respecting private returns after investment. A fiscal authority must finance a given expenditure from labor and capital income. Ordinary tax receipts are protected, but an opportunistic executive can seize part of the remaining capital payment. We show that a revenue-neutral increase in the capital tax raises the probability of compliance whenever the labor tax is below its local, fixedwage revenue peak, provided the equilibrium remains on a regular mixing branch. This result does not depend on the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor. The same reform can raise investment: the gain in expected retention must outweigh the decline in the opportunist’s continuation gain as compliance becomes less informative. We also characterize the Ramsey allocation conditional on full compliance. Limited commitment then imposes a ceiling on sustainable capital payments, rather than a general lower bound on the statutory capital-tax rate. Finally, we distinguish a change in the authority’s concern for the future from an increase in both actors’ patience. The former favors more informative policies when continuation welfare is convex; the latter has no unconditional direction in the reduced-form policy problem.

ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.title: Tax Expenditure Reporting as a Commitment Device for Revenue Mobilization
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.author: Gaël Tape
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.summary: This note shows that publishing tax expenditure reports increases tax revenue mobilization over the medium term in emerging and developing countries. The results indicate that this effect emerges six to seven years after publication and is driven primarily by direct taxes. The effect is stronger when reports are published more frequently and on a regular basis. It is also more pronounced in low-income countries and in sub-Saharan Africa. Publishing tax expenditure reports acts as a commitment mechanism. By making tax exemptions visible, it raises the political cost of opaque exemptions and gradually strengthens the government's capacity to steer tax policy.

ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.title: The Strange and Curious Tax Treatment of Investment Expenses
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.author: Morris, Mallory A.
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.summary: To secure income, taxpayers often incur a wide range of expenses. At least theoretically, one might think that the Internal Revenue Code (“Code”) would accord all such expenses similar tax treatment, but (i) trade or business expenses and (ii) investment expenses endure the exact opposite tax treatment: the former are generally allowed, whereas the latter are commonly disallowed. The obvious question is why there is a difference in treatment between the two. This Article explores possible answers to that important question. It first traces the evolution of the Code’s dichotomous tax treatment of trade or business versus investment expenses. It then investigates possible justifications and their associated merits for the different handling of these two expense categories. With this background information in mind, to make the tax system more administrable, equitable, and efficient, this Article advocates for the deductibility of investment expenses and describes several beneficial implications associated with the institution of this proposed reform

ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.title: Workplace Transformation And Its Tax Compliance Implications
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.author: Soled, Jay A.
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.summary: Due to technological advances and the COVID-19 pandemic, taxpayers are increasingly utilizing their homes as a focal point from which to conduct their business affairs. On the one hand, the nation should applaud this workplace transformation insofar as it may enhance job performance and efficiency, reduce product cost and overhead, and improve work-life balance. On the other hand, this transformation process may open the door to rampant tax abuse as taxpayers alone or in collusion with their employers seek to transform home usage into a tax shelter refuge. This analysis delves directly into the income tax compliance concerns that the workplace transformation engenders. It does so by exposing the nature of the problem, its prevalence, what it might cost the nation annually in terms of lost revenue, and why current safeguards are failing to achieve their sought-after objectives. The good news is that if Congress proactively takes immediate remedial measures to address this nascent problem, such actions could help foster taxpayer compliance, defend the income tax base, and halt the depletion of the nation’s revenue coffers. However, if Congress dallies and is derelict in fulfilling its oversight duties, this problem is poised to go from bad to worse.

1e604061d7:65c15d9c56ff3a02.title: Whistleblowers and Disinformation — Roundtable #2: The Public Sector
1e604061d7:65c15d9c56ff3a02.author: Diane Ring

b0a91b96f4:a484eaa198cae704.title: The Cost of Human Frailty: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Test!
b0a91b96f4:a484eaa198cae704.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:a484eaa198cae704.summary: In a month full of big stories, perhaps the biggest business story was the fall from grace of Jensen Huang and the consequences for Nvidia, investors, and the rest of the AI trade. The initial story, with its potent mix of personal fallibility and security concerns, related to Jensen’s affair with Alice Huang, who news stories labeled a Chinese spy, though the evidence on the ground is still thin. I had planned to write about the story then, but on the road in Asia and with teaching commitments, I put it off for a few days, and over those days, the story took a turn, with stories of dalliances with Nvidia employees. Last week culminated with Nvidia’s board asking Jensen to step down, and his agreeing, perhaps bringing to an end one of the more eventful and productive stints as a CEO in corporate history. I have no desire or standing to debate the moral aspects of this story, and I will let others take sides on whether the board should or should not have fired Jensen. In this post, I will focus on the question of what Jensen stepping down as CEO might mean for Nvidia’s value, and whether after the market correction over the last three weeks, the market has overreached. What does a CEO do? What does a CEO do for a business? Given the many tasks that go into creating, building, and running a business, it should come as no surprise that the list is long, but I will classify them broadly into groups: Storyteller: Every business is built around a story, and that story drives its valuation and sometimes its pricing. While that story is grounded in the company’s products and the markets that it seeks, it is the top manager’s job to craft and tell the story to investors, employees and to consumers. Clearly, the significance of this component of a CEO’s story will shift, depending on where the company is in its life cycle, with its importance being greatest at either end of the life cycle. I promised that I would return to complete the per share valuation, when the details were made available, and an updated prospectus filed last week filled that gap. The world has not stayed still in the fifteen days since my original valuation, and both company-level and macro developments require an update to my valuation. The prospectus was updated to include third quarter numbers, and the midterm elections have potentially altered the economics of the AI business, as data centers may become more difficult and expensive to build and AI regulations may become more stringent. In this post, I will start with a general discussion of how share count is complicated by the existence of multiple classes of shares and stock-based compensation, and argue that the absence of standardization has made share count the Wild West in investing, with consequences for both intrinsic valuation and pricing. I will then update my valuation of Anthropic and assess the per share value, based on the prospectus that was just filed. The Elusive Share Count When I first started valuing companies, getting from aggregate value to equity value per share was a trivial exercise, where you divided the aggregate value by the number of shares outstanding. This was, of course, a period when almost every US company had only one class of shares and stock-based compensation was still in its nascent stages, and lightly used. That is no longer the case, and while tedious, I think that the process of understanding share count has to start with the basics of what goes into that number for publicly traded companies. b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.summary: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. I plan to play devil's advocate with my own valuation, looking at my story inputs, and ranking them in order of fragility, partly to stress-test my value estimate and partly to reinforce some corporate finance first principles, and then move on to your feedback and what I take away from it. b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.summary: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs) rather than total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. 1aa97d921e:a6c5935f96497651.summary: In new research, Nicholas Short, Sophie Hill, and Jacob Brown examine "ideological capture": regulatory capture that works not through lobbying but through experts defining what goals and values regulators may consider. Surveying the public alongside antitrust lawyers, they find the consumer welfare standard marginalizes important public concerns, like the risk of increased layoffs or more lobbying power. 1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.title: Anti-Monopoly as Industrial Policy: The Chicago School Versus Adam Smith
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.author: Richard R. John
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.summary: Jolted by the Great Depression of the 1930s, Thurman Arnold devised an anti-monopoly industrial policy for the United States Justice Department that breathed fresh life into a then-moribund Sherman Anti-Trust Act. Arnold’s jurisprudence built on Adam Smith’s discovery that market-making could promote national security and forestall civil unrest. Smith’s insights had informed the industrial policy of Alexander Hamilton, who laid the groundwork in the 1790s for the country’s economic development. Edward H. Levi brought Arnold’s pragmatic anti-monopolism to the University of Chicago. Here, ironically, Arnoldian jurisprudence would be transmogrified into the doctrinaire company-over-country market fundamentalism of the Chicago School of Economics. Today, writes Richard R. John, as we envision for the 21st century a new pro-market, pro-freedom, pro-national security industrial policy, it is worth recalling how U. S. economic development took the form that it did, why the Chicago School repudiated the enduring wisdom of Adam Smith, and what this portends for the world of today. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.title: How George Stigler and the Chicago School Opened the Marketplace of Ideas to Business
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.author: Edward Nik-Khah
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.summary: Henry Simons, the “Crown Prince” of the Chicago School and a professor in the economics department and the law school prior to World War II, sought to develop a laissez faire economics program devoted to eliminating monopoly and pursuing egalitarian goals. George Stigler and the Chicago School abandoned Simons’s anti-monopoly and egalitarian program. The best market became one driven by the search for profits, and the best-functioning marketplace of ideas arose where winning ideas reflected the greater funding backing them, writes Edward Nik-Khah. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.title: The Chicago School Abandoned the Positive Freedom of Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.author: Maha Rafi Atal
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.summary: Adam Smith’s theory of political economy did not begin with the isolated individual but rather the individual who operates to earn the respect of others. Wealth and freedom grew from these relationships and engaging with others to create a free society, or what 20th century philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s would call positive freedom. In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Chicago School abandoned this aspect of freedom in preference of the isolated individual, which in turn produced a weaker concept of freedom, morality, and society that has stifled the cultivation of all three in the United States, writes Maha Rafi Atal. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.title: Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy Complicates Interpretations by the Chicago School and Its Critics
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.author: Sandra Peart and David Levy
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.summary: The connections between Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Theory of Moral Sentiments reveal a much more complicated understanding of how markets work than developed in the common interpretation by the Chicago School of economics or that of its critics. Smith’s political economy based on commerce, sympathy, and competition produced social good but only when complemented and checked by other forces. When not checked, Smith worried about “factions” that produce bad outcomes, write Sandra J. Peart and David M. Levy. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.title: Why Economics Forsook Democracy
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.author: Robert Van Horn
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.summary: The post-World War II Chicago School of Aaron Director and Milton Friedman reimagined a new (neo) liberalism that treated economic liberties and the free market as the greatest defense of political rights. The government, and democracy, were more often than not barriers to economic liberties. The United States continues to suffer from neoliberalism’s prescriptions, and addressing the concerns of today’s populist movements will mean rediscovering ideas of freedom that the Chicago School denigrated, writes Robert Van Horn. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.title: The University of Chicago Once Studied a Laissez-Faire Economics Compatible with Public Interest
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.author: David Mitch
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.summary: The Chicago School is often associated with laissez-faire economics that reads into Adam Smith’s philosophy of political economy justifications for self-interest and prudential motivations. However, a careful history of the University of Chicago’s early Economics Department and School of Commerce and Administration reveals a more complicated understanding of how economics and business were to interact with one another and society. The early University of Chicago pursued a program that emphasized that laissez-faire economics and a concern for the public interest were not antagonists but perfectly compatible, writes David Mitch.
