59ec699e9f:8af8334c8538ebd8.title: Artificial intelligence and work organisation
59ec699e9f:8af8334c8538ebd8.author: Eurofound
59ec699e9f:8af8334c8538ebd8.summary: Using the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) and the European Working Conditions Survey (EWCS), this paper examines the relationship between occupational exposure to Artificial Intelligence (AI) and changes in work organisation between roughly 2011 and 2024, a period that encompasses the early diffusion of generative AI. Work organisation has evolved over this period, with manual tasks declining, problem-solving and information-processing tasks becoming more prevalent, and teamwork becoming increasingly common. AI may have played some role in these changes: occupations more exposed to AI have seen a smaller increase in monotonous tasks, while the frequency of some information-processing tasks has increased faster. That being said, rising educational attainment appears to have played a more significant role in some of these changes in work organisation, underscoring the continued importance of investments in education and training.

59ec699e9f:e7e064427c58bce1.title: Earnings inequality as an investor issue: A framework for engagement
59ec699e9f:e7e064427c58bce1.author: OECD
59ec699e9f:e7e064427c58bce1.summary: This paper explores the corporate, governance and institutional factors that shape earnings inequality and assesses the extent to which investors can influence these drivers through stewardship and engagement. Drawing on evidence from the literature and cross-country analysis, it identifies six pathways linking company practices and labour market institutions to earnings outcomes, and proposes a framework of metrics to support investor decision-making and engagement.

59ec699e9f:33138546632977cf.title: Sorting into Entrepreneurial Teams
59ec699e9f:33138546632977cf.author: Marta Morazzoni
59ec699e9f:33138546632977cf.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form. Cet article examine comment les entrepreneurs s’associent pour former des équipes fondatrices et comment la composition de ces équipes façonne la distribution des entreprises. Nous développons une théorie du choix de carrière et de la formation des équipes dans laquelle les complémentarités entre compétences rendent l’entrepreneuriat en équipe attrayant pour les individus aux profils de compétences déséquilibrés, tandis que la similitude des niveaux de talent rend cette option préférable à d’autres choix de carrière. À partir de données portugaises appariant employeurs et employés ainsi que de données de bilan, nous montrons que les équipes combinant des niveaux de talent similaires et des spécialisations diversifiées créent des entreprises plus grandes, plus productives et dont la durée de vie est plus longue. Pourtant, les fondateurs aux compétences différentes sont moins susceptibles de créer une entreprise ensemble. Nous calibrons…

59ec699e9f:19c28f2ab9399116.title: Networks and Queues: Evidence from Medical Referrals in Canada
59ec699e9f:19c28f2ab9399116.author: Maripier Isabelle
59ec699e9f:19c28f2ab9399116.summary: When prices are fixed, queues become central allocation mechanisms. Yet decentralized waiting queues are often unobserved, creating inefficiencies and the opportunity for informal access through referral networks. This paper studies a 2016 reform in Quebec, Canada, that introduced a centralized system for allocating medical referrals from general practitioners to physician specialists. We find that centralization significantly reduced new specialist consultations. We also infer physician referral networks and estimate a structural model that enables us to conclude that specialists tend to defer consultations for patients referred by general practitioners from whom they receive an unusually large number of referrals. Lorsque les prix sont fixes, les files d’attente deviennent des mécanismes centraux d’allocation des ressources. Toutefois, les files d’attente décentralisées sont souvent difficiles à observer, ce qui engendre des inefficacités et crée des possibilités d’accès informel par l’intermédiaire des réseaux de référence médicale. Cet article étudie une réforme mise en œuvre en 2016 au Québec, au Canada, qui a instauré un système centralisé d’attribution des demandes de consultation adressées par les médecins généralistes aux médecins spécialistes. Nous constatons que cette centralisation a entraîné une réduction statistiquement significative du nombre de nouvelles consultations auprès de médecins spécialistes. Nous reconstituons également les réseaux de référence entre médecins et estimons un modèle structurel qui nous permet de conclure que les médecins spécialistes ont tendance à reporter les consultations des patients orientés par des médecins généralistes dont ils reçoivent un nombre inhabituellement élevé de demandes de consultation.

59ec699e9f:1eae2d61e541a1b2.title: Institutional Transmission of Social Preferences
59ec699e9f:1eae2d61e541a1b2.author: Julen Zarate-Pina
59ec699e9f:1eae2d61e541a1b2.summary: Using incentivized experiments with 2854 primary school students and 238 teachers, we study how teachers’ social preferences shape students’ own prosociality. Leveraging within-school variation in teachers’ social preferences, we show that students taught by more prosocial teachers give more in a dictator game, contribute more in a public goods game, and report lower outcomes in a die-reporting task, even after controlling for students’ cognitive skills, personality traits and socio-economic background. The relationship is larger among older students, consistent with teachers’ influence accumulating through continued interaction, while peer dynamics and students’ beliefs emerge as potential channels for the transmission of social preferences. Our findings highlight the role of teachers as key institutional agents of prosocial development.

59ec699e9f:fcd1cdfcc2920ccf.title: Effects of Local Demand Shocks
59ec699e9f:fcd1cdfcc2920ccf.author: Bergström, Balder
59ec699e9f:fcd1cdfcc2920ccf.summary: This paper concerns the effects of labour demand shocks on the local labour market stemming from plant expansions. I use both a Two Stage Difference in Difference estimator and a Synthetic Difference in Difference estimator to find how a large plant expansion or opening affects the local labour market.

59ec699e9f:2d0381c3437a23fd.title: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
59ec699e9f:2d0381c3437a23fd.author: Alexander Plum
59ec699e9f:2d0381c3437a23fd.summary: This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.

59ec699e9f:45afbf682fbf3ba6.title: Dynamic Individuals, Static Neighborhoods: Migration and Earnings Changes in Poor Neighborhoods
59ec699e9f:45afbf682fbf3ba6.author: Bryan Stuart
59ec699e9f:45afbf682fbf3ba6.summary: Why do poor neighborhoods stay poor? Using administrative data linking residential histories to longitudinal earnings, we show that while many residents of poor neighborhoods have persistently low earnings and remain in concentrated poverty for extended periods, a large number also experience sizable earnings growth and move to richer areas. Estimates based on idiosyncratic, firm-specific pay changes show that part of this sorting is causal — earnings increases induce upward moves. On net, selective migration depresses the growth of poor neighborhoods’ average earnings by roughly 60 percent and represents an underappreciated driver of the persistence of concentrated poverty.

59ec699e9f:b40521bb275a5d32.title: Ph.D. Enrollment and the Option Value of Industrial Careers
59ec699e9f:b40521bb275a5d32.author: Airi Hayama
59ec699e9f:b40521bb275a5d32.summary: Japan promotes doctoral education by providing financial support to Ph.D. students and encouraging firms to hire graduates. To evaluate these policies, this paper develops a heterogeneous agent macroeconomic model in which Ph.D. graduates can work in the industrial sector as well as in the academic sector. In general equilibrium, the industrial-sector career option barely works as insurance for students who aim for an academic career. In the economy with this career option, a student subsidy generates a larger increase in overall enrollment than a hiring subsidy of the same fiscal cost. The hiring subsidy instead moves some students who would have entered academia into industry and raises aggregate output. These results suggest that the choice between these fiscal policies should depend on whether the goal is to attract new Ph.D. students or to change the careers of those who would enroll anyway.

59ec699e9f:de43858099f63a66.title: Severance pay reforms, worker flows, and labor market duality
59ec699e9f:de43858099f63a66.author: de Almeida Vilares, Hugo
59ec699e9f:de43858099f63a66.summary: This paper studies how cuts to statutory severance pay affect worker flows, contractual allocation, firm-level hiring composition, and wages in the Portuguese labor market. The analysis exploits the 2011-2013 reforms, which reduced the transfer component of dismissal protection for both fixed-term and open-ended contracts while leaving most procedural safeguards intact. Using matched employer-employee data for 2010?2019, we combine sharp legal-timing contrasts around the November 2011 and October 2013 cutoffs with an exposure-based IV/control-function design that leverages heterogeneity in admission cohort, tenure, contract type, and grandfathered rights. The results show that lower severance pay does not uniformly improve reallocation. Around the November 2011 cutoff, separations shift away from exits from private-sector employment toward job-to-job moves, whereas the October 2013 cutoff does not reproduce this pattern, instead displaying weaker job-to-job responses and a more uneven reduction in exits. In the broader exposure estimates, lower severance entitlements are associated with higher turnover, but the composition of that turnover varies across worker groups and contract types, combining selective conversion from fixed-term to open-ended jobs with increased reliance on temporary contracts. Within continuing worker-firm matches, wage-severance associations are economically small, providing little evidence that lower severance rights were offset by higher wages. Overall, the reforms reshaped turnover and contract use without delivering uniform improvements in labor-market reallocation, and temporary-permanent duality remains a central feature of the post-reform labor market.

59ec699e9f:fb281726f601ad59.title: Specialization vs. Diversification: Research Strategy and Performance in Economics
59ec699e9f:fb281726f601ad59.author: Christian Zimmermann
59ec699e9f:fb281726f601ad59.summary: The tension between diversification and specialization is a central theme in economics, shaping discourse in fields as disparate as international trade, portfolio theory, and corporate scope. This paper examines this trade-off within the realm of research strategy. Using the RePEc panel database of approximately 60, 000 economists, we demonstrate that the pursuit of a diversified research portfolio yields superior performance as measured by citations and publications as well as lower research attrition rates. This advantage applies to both senior and, in contrast to conventional wisdom, early-career researchers. This strategy is significantly facilitated by joint work with new co-authors.

59ec699e9f:6246afcca8e163ee.title: Minimum Wage, Business Dynamism, and the Life Cycle of Firms
59ec699e9f:6246afcca8e163ee.author: Alexandre Sollaci
59ec699e9f:6246afcca8e163ee.summary: This paper studies the effects of the minimum wage on the life cycle of firms. We start by building a tractable model where heterogeneous firms have labor market power, invest in innovation, and choose formal or informal sectors. The model predicts that a minimum wage hike not only shrinks the young and lower-productivity firms but also decreases the incentives to innovate, resulting in slower life-cycle growth. We show that these predictions hold in Brazilian administrative and census data, leveraging the variation in exposure to the minimum wage between 1999 and 2010. An increase in the minimum wage (i) decreases the growth rates of small and young establishments and (ii) increases the growth rates of old and large establishments. At the municipal level, we observe an increase in informal employment and in the earnings of both formal and informal workers. Lastly, we augment our simple model into a full quantitative general equilibrium model with monopsonistic firms, endogenous innovation, and formal-informal choice, calibrated to the Brazilian economy. A counterfactual minimum wage increase generates reallocation from young to old firms, dampens innovation at low-productivity firms, and expands the informal sector. Our findings suggest that the minimum wage is a possible explanation for the decline in the importance of young establishments and business dynamism in Brazil.

59ec699e9f:20c7efb300146bc7.title: Labor Market Tightness and Minority Earnings Gaps
59ec699e9f:20c7efb300146bc7.author: Victor Hernandez Martinez
59ec699e9f:20c7efb300146bc7.summary: We study how labor-market tightness affects minority earnings gaps using administrative data for US metropolitan areas from 2010 to 2025. After accounting for national shocks, local seasonality, and local trends, a 1-percentage-point unemployment decline reduces the white-minus-minority earnings gap by about 0.2 percentage points for all jobs and 0.3 percentage points for new stable hires. These responses strengthen as slack declines, reaching 0.4 and 0.6 percentage points, respectively, in hot markets. Neither observed worker and vacancy composition nor concurrent policy changes account for these effects. Increased mobility and upgrading across broad job categories explain little of the narrowing, although hiring distributions become more similar between the two groups. Where recruiting is concentrated among fewer employers, the earnings-gap response varies less with slack. Together, the findings point toward relative earnings improvements within labor-market segments and employer competition as a mechanism through which tightness narrows minority earnings gaps.

59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.title: Supporting into-work benefit reform in Spain
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.author: OECD
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.summary: In Spain, the Complemento de Apoyo al Empleo (CAE) allows individuals to receive unemployment benefits whilst in employment. This paper sets out the findings and recommendations of a project aimed at improving the CAE, drawing on international good practice, as well as analyses carried out using the OECD TaxBen model and administrative data. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance – by linking its amount either to UI entitlements or directly to the previous wage – would provide stronger work incentives when wage loss at re-employment is greater; and would limit low-wage traps for full-time workers. However, such reforms would tend to offer lower net income and weaker work incentives for workers transitioning between two low-paid jobs, compared with the current CAE. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance would also increase CAE coverage among re-employed individuals and, consequently, fiscal costs, albeit to a moderate extent. Higher CAE coverage would particularly benefit certain vulnerable groups whose coverage is currently relatively low, such as the low skilled, the youth, and workers in southern regions.

59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.title: Return-to-Work Policies for Disability Insurance Recipients: The Role of Financial Incentives
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.author: Tojerow, Ilan
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.summary: This paper studies how financial incentives shape labor supply decisions among disability insurance (DI) recipients who already combine benefits with part-time work. We exploit a distinctive feature of the Belgian Adapted Work Program, in which DI benefits are progressively withdrawn as earnings increase and the marginal withdrawal rate rises sharply at predefined thresholds. Because participants cannot freely adjust their working hours, this setting allows us to estimate how higher implicit taxation affects transitions out of partial work. Using administrative data and a Regression Kink Design, we find that higher implicit tax rates induce exits in two opposite directions: toward full-time employment and back to full DI. A oneeuro increase in the implicit marginal tax per working day raises the probability of returning to full DI by 3.0 percentage points and of resuming full-time employment by 1.5 percentage points, corresponding to elasticities of 0.84 and 0.85. A simple labor supply framework rationalizes these divergent responses. Our findings show that the financial design of partial-benefit schemes can determine whether partial work serves as a bridge toward full employment or instead leads recipients back to full benefit dependency.

59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.title: Earnings Dynamics under Firm Heterogeneity
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.author: Timo Virtanen
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.summary: We develop a permanent–transitory earnings process in which permanent shocks depend on a latent firm type and workers’ exposure to firm types is persistent. Persistence can substantially slow the finite-horizon attenuation of earnings skewness and excess kurtosis over the life cycle relative to an iid mixture benchmark. We estimate the model from matched employer-employee data, first grouping firms based on the distribution of residual earnings changes and then using worker transitions across groups to estimate persistence. Finnish data reveal heterogeneity in permanent-shock variances and persistent exposure to firm groups. Although skewness and excess kurtosis are not targeted in estimation, over ages 35–50 the extended model accounts for 49 percent of average empirical skewness and 39 percent of average excess kurtosis, compared with 4 percent and 3 percent under the iid benchmark. Quantitative exercises show that persistence increases the life-cycle cost of earnings risk and affects saving behavior.

59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.title: Informal Work as a Fallback: Vision Impairment, Employment, and Policy in Brazil
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.author: Marcio V. Correa
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.summary: Informal work may allow workers with functional limitations to remain employed when formal jobs become too costly to hold, rather than reflecting exclusion from good jobs. In Brazilâ€™s 2019 Pesquisa Nacional de Saude, severe but partial vision impairment is associated with a formal employment rate 20.9 percentage points lower than among individuals with no difficulty, but with no difference in informal employment. The asymmetry survives adjustment for observables and other functional limitations, and it is not shared by mobility, upper-limb, or mental limitations. These patterns alone cannot reveal where affected workers would go if informal work were unavailable, or how policy would reallocate them. To answer these questions, we build a general-equilibrium incomplete-markets model in which individuals choose among formal work, informal work, and non-employment. Informal work is less productive, while formal work carries a rigidity cost that rises with functional limitation. We calibrate the model to occupational shares across four vision states. In the model, eliminating informal work lowers employment by 17.6 percentage points among individuals with a vision limitation. In illustrative counterfactuals, policies that reduce informality send workers to different destinations: stricter enforcement into non-employment, workplace accommodation into formal jobs, and broader disability-benefit eligibility into supported non-employment. Changes in informality are therefore an unreliable guide to the effects of disability and formalization policy.

59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.title: Do Firms Know What Workers Want?
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.author: Max Müller
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.summary: Labor supply depends on wages and amenities, and standard models implicitly assume that firms hold accurate beliefs about workers’ amenity valuations. In a survey with firms and workers in Germany linked to administrative data, we measure workers’ valuations of five different amenities and firms’ beliefs about workers’ valuations. We find that firms systematically underestimate workers’ valuations of all five amenities. These misperceptions are driven by interpersonal projection: managers project their own preferences—they value amenities less—onto workers. Through the lens of a simple model of imperfect competition, we show that firm misperceptions result in (i) labor shortages and (ii) excess labor costs for biased firms. Empirical tests confirm these predictions: a simple calibration suggests that non-providing firms could reduce their labor costs by 5% by providing amenities.

59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.author: Ana Popovici
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

59ec699e9f:564c604d25e17358.title: Exposure Is Not Adoption: Measuring Generative AI and Labor Demand
59ec699e9f:564c604d25e17358.author: Ashish K. Sedai
59ec699e9f:564c604d25e17358.summary: Occupational exposure indices measure what generative AI could do, not what it is used for. I build a behavioral measure of realized AI adoption from the Anthropic Economic Index and compare it with the standard exposure index across 47 occupational sectors. Adoption and exposure rank occupations alike but diverge in level, because adoption is far more concentrated. In weekly Indeed job postings after ChatGPT, labor demand tracks adoption rather than exposure: a one standard deviation increase in adoption predicts a decline of about 10 log points, while exposure adds nothing. A second adoption measure, built from OpenAI usage, reproduces the pattern, so the result is not specific to one model family. Realized adoption captures AI's early labor market footprint.

59ec699e9f:93c511051db2583e.title: How is AI Affecting College Major and Course Choices? Evidence from Finland
59ec699e9f:93c511051db2583e.author: Tuomas P. Heikkinen
59ec699e9f:93c511051db2583e.summary: Have concerns about the potential job displacement effects of artificial intelligence affected the education choices of students? We analyze administrative data on the university applications and course choices of Finnish students. We find, after the launch of ChatGPT 3.5 in November 2022, a persistent drop in applications to fields of study classified as more exposed to AI under several different measures. The drop is particularly large in computer science and other ICT fields. Examining the elective course choices of non-ICT students, we find declining enrollment in programming and algorithms courses, particularly among students who had not taken mathematics as part of their high school exit exam. At the same time, non-ICT students enrolled more in AI/ML courses, and this increase was relatively larger among men.

59ec699e9f:8e1ea7f034167396.title: Estimating, Bounding, and Decomposing the Effects of a Parent-Directed School Readiness Program
59ec699e9f:8e1ea7f034167396.author: Rui Zeng
59ec699e9f:8e1ea7f034167396.summary: We evaluate JumpStart, a parent-directed school-readiness program run by a Houston-area school district, in a randomized trial spanning three cohorts. Being offered the program raises scores on a curriculum-aligned assessment by 7.6 percentage points and parental investment by 0.26 standard deviations. A model of skill formation with endogenous inputs and program participation yields an average treatment effect of completing the program of about 9 percentage points, and attributes roughly a quarter of this effect to higher measured investment. Nonparametric bounds corroborate the average effect, and a mediation analysis that relaxes part of the model's structure supports the decomposition.

59ec699e9f:c2bb505657b5f067.title: Who Feels the Boom? Labor Market Tightness and the Heterogeneous Employment Effects of Monetary Policy
59ec699e9f:c2bb505657b5f067.author: Michael Weber
59ec699e9f:c2bb505657b5f067.summary: We study how monetary policy affects employment across workers with differing labor-force attachment. Exploiting local labor-market variation, we find that monetary easing disproportionately boosts employment among Black workers, less-educated workers, and women in tighter markets, as measured by the prime-age employment-to-population ratio. A one-standard-deviation federal funds rate cut raises two-year Black employment growth by 0.6 percentage points more in markets at the 90th than the 10th percentile of tightness. These differences persist and are amplified by greater monetary-policy exposure. A model with heterogeneous workers shows how tightness shapes hiring composition while policy exposure determines demand responses. Tightness primarily shapes the distribution, not the magnitude, of employment gains.

59ec699e9f:685fba10197f47b3.title: How do Top Earners Respond to Taxation? Own- and Cross-Tax Base Responses, Efficiency, and Inequality
59ec699e9f:685fba10197f47b3.author: Horacio Rueda
59ec699e9f:685fba10197f47b3.summary: This paper presents new evidence on how top income earners respond to changes in the personal labor income tax schedule, uncovering both own- and cross-tax base responses within a unified framework. For identification, we exploit a 2012 tax reform in Uruguay that generated quasi-random variation in top marginal rates within the top 1% of the labor income distribution. Our empirical approach relies on a difference-in-differences identification strategy and administrative records linked at the individual level across multiple tax bases. We estimate an own-tax base intensive margin elasticity of 0.82 and extensive margin semi-elasticity of 3.36. Extensive margin responses are mostly driven by taxpayers shifting from the personal labor income tax base toward corporate income or capital income tax bases (semi-elasticities of -1.00 and -0.61, respectively). Our preferred estimates suggest that the reform was effective in increasing tax revenues, with efficiency costs representing 31% of the projected increase. However, it had limited impact on inequality, most likely due to its narrow scope and income shifting toward tax bases with lower and flat rates. Overall, our results indicate that policy efforts aiming to reduce inequality by increasing top marginal tax rates should also focus on limiting income shifting opportunities to strengthen their redistributive effects.

59ec699e9f:b834c167e8395384.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
59ec699e9f:b834c167e8395384.author: María Micaela Sviatschi
59ec699e9f:b834c167e8395384.summary: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2, 500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

59ec699e9f:4c987ede61749ce4.title: Occupational sorting as a mechanism of persistent inequality in South Africa
59ec699e9f:4c987ede61749ce4.author: Mdluli, Mlondi Mveli
59ec699e9f:4c987ede61749ce4.summary: Three decades after the end of formal job reservation, who reaches the top of South Africa’s occupational hierarchy remains sharply divided by race. This paper provides the first systematic decomposition of racial gaps in occupational access in South Africa. Using harmonised PALMS v4 data for 1993, 2003, 2013 and 2025, it estimates a pooled multinomial logit of low-, mid- and high-skill placement with race-by-year and gender-by-year interactions. It then applies Fairlie non-linear decompositions to separate the gap in high-skill placement into a component explained by education, age, location and public-sector employment and an unexplained residual. Gender gaps are decomposed separately within each racial group. The results show a “sticky floor” that has loosened and a “glass ceiling” that has tightened. Racial gaps in low-skill placement narrowed for African/Black and Coloured workers. The gap at the top widened: African/Black workers’ odds of high-skill placement relative to White workers fell from 46 to 71 per cent lower, and the probability gap rose from 35.7 to 45.0 percentage points. Roughly three-fifths of this gap remains unexplained after 2003, while Indian/Asian workers converge substantially. Women across all racial groups moved from relative advantage in 1993 to disadvantage by 2025. Public-sector employment partially moderated these gaps rather than generating them. Because the model has only five covariates, the unexplained component is consistent with structural barriers but does not prove them. The findings suggest that occupational sorting is a mechanism through which post-apartheid inequality persists.

59ec699e9f:a133c0618e60b014.title: Pricing Intelligence: Task-Based Learning and Labor Displacement in the AI Economy
59ec699e9f:a133c0618e60b014.author: Carl-Christian Groh
59ec699e9f:a133c0618e60b014.summary: What determines the speed of AI-driven labor displacement? I study this question in a microeconomic model in which users choose between labor and AI to complete tasks. AI models improve through task-specific learning from deployment. Profit-maximizing AI providers optimally price tasks where labor has a strong comparative advantage out of automation to extract more revenue from other tasks, which decelerates aggregate AI adoption by preventing AI learning on the excluded tasks. I characterize when this tension gives rise to an accelerating path of AI adoption or a learning trap. Competi tion can accelerate AI adoption by shifting AI deployment and learning toward tasks where AI has a comparative disadvantage, even though it reduces each provider’s total data access. Asymmetric competition can further accelerate AI adoption by inducing providers to specialize. Importantly, even temporary regulatory interventions such as constraints on providers’ compute capacities can keep AI adoption persistently low.

59ec699e9f:2d5bcfd3407e5304.title: Financial Advisors and Retirees' Risk-taking
59ec699e9f:2d5bcfd3407e5304.author: Noah Stoffman
59ec699e9f:2d5bcfd3407e5304.summary: Advised retirees keep about two-thirds of their portfolios in equities well into old age—30 to 40 percentage points more than non-advised retirees, target-date funds, or common rules of thumb. These allocations reflect active choices rather than inertia, and they adjust gradually toward a new advisor’s investment style following advisor switches. Equity shares rise with relationship tenure, and advisor influence is strongest among clients with low financial knowledge or risk tolerance, consistent with trust facilitating risk-taking. Given retirees’ modest financial wealth relative to their safe pension income, we rationalize these portfolios in a standard life-cycle model with moderate risk aversion. Modeling advisors as “money doctors” who correct clients’ pessimistic beliefs about the equity premium, we find that, relative to a no-advice counterfactual, the welfare gains from higher risk-taking are of the same order of magnitude as the cost of advice.

59ec699e9f:b4ce9ce00b44c25a.title: The Impact of AI Diffusion on the Labor Market: Task Shifts in Occupational Labor Demand
59ec699e9f:b4ce9ce00b44c25a.author: Jinyeong Yun
59ec699e9f:b4ce9ce00b44c25a.summary: This paper studies how the diffusion of AI changes the demand for labor across occupations in Korea. We extend the task-based decomposition of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) to the occupation level, estimate displacement and reinstatement for each cell of occupation and industry by projecting changes in wage-bill shares on AI exposure, and feed the estimated task shifts into a model of occupational choice. We find that reinstatement has been larger than displacement, so that the net task shift favors labor. The overall effect is accordingly a mild improvement: wages rise by 2.1 percent and welfare by 1.7 percent on average. The effects are far from uniform, however. The dispersion of wage changes across occupations is more than six times the mean, and because occupational mobility is low, the adjustment comes mostly through wages rather than reallocation. Among workers below the age of 60, those with a college degree or higher gain considerably more than those without, and prime-age workers with lower educational attainment gain the least. Although every age-education group gains on average, 43 percent of workers experience welfare losses, and whether a worker loses depends mainly on the occupation in which the worker starts rather than on age or education. Earnings gains are concentrated at the bottom and the top of the distribution.

59ec699e9f:dfb8508e64b9784b.title: What pays beyond the degree? A systematic review of educational credentials and early-career earnings
59ec699e9f:dfb8508e64b9784b.author: Stijn Baert
59ec699e9f:dfb8508e64b9784b.summary: Students must allocate their time during tertiary education, but the evidence on the earnings value of their achievements and experiences is dispersed across separate literatures. We systematically reviewed 38 quantitative studies examining academic performance, delayed graduation, internship experience, student employment, and student leadership in relation to earnings during the first five years after graduation. We distinguish correlational evidence from quasi-experimental estimates and interpret the findings against theoretical mechanisms linking credentials to earnings. We find that academic performance is generally positively associated with earnings and has the most consistent quasi-experimental support for earnings premiums, especially at labour market entry. Internships can also yield substantial earnings gains, but estimates vary more across programmes and research designs. Student employment is generally associated with higher earnings when field-related, but the evidence does not establish a general causal premium. Delayed graduation and student leadership remain comparatively understudied. Student guidance should therefore consider the characteristics and context of specific credentials, alongside the strength of the evidence on earnings benefits.

59ec699e9f:9984d0532fbf7713.title: Labor Supply Frictions and Optimal Long-Run Fiscal Policy
59ec699e9f:9984d0532fbf7713.author: Youngsoo Jang
59ec699e9f:9984d0532fbf7713.summary: We study how labor supply frictions documented in micro data shape Ramsey-optimal long-run fiscal policy in an economy with uninsurable idiosyncratic risk. Households choose whether and how much to work, subject to a fixed cost of work and a constraint that bunches hours at the standard workweek, two frictions that originate outside fiscal policy. The government discounts the future at the households' rate. Examining how employment and hours respond before, at, and after an anticipated tax increase, we find that an interior candidate Ramsey steady state arises only when the participation margin is combined with the fixed cost. Without them, as in recent work, households work more before the tax takes effect, and the tax approaches a confiscatory 100 percent. With them, the fall in employment when the tax takes effect outweighs the anticipatory rise, and the fixed cost widens the gap. The hours constraint dampens the anticipatory rise and lowers the long-run tax to about 69 percent.

59ec699e9f:e751e0a56fb3fff6.title: Visa Quotas, Undocumented Migration, and Skill Selection
59ec699e9f:e751e0a56fb3fff6.author: Giorgio Fabbri
59ec699e9f:e751e0a56fb3fff6.summary: We study how expanding official migration channels affects the size and composition of inflows when individuals with heterogeneous income choose between staying, applying for a rationed legal visa, or attempting undocumented migration. We characterize the equilibrium sorting, showing that official channels attract intermediate-income agents while the undocumented route attracts those with lower incomes. Increasing visa quotas replaces a mass of undocumented migrants with official applicants: while this shift reduces irregularity and alters the skill composition of arrivals, we find that it can paradoxically reduce the total number of migrants. This “crowding-in reversal” occurs when the policy triggers an excessive displacement from the always-accessible undocumented path to the rationed official lottery.

59ec699e9f:43630dd1626245c2.title: Reverse Gender Bias in Performance Ratings
59ec699e9f:43630dd1626245c2.author: Asri Özgümüs
59ec699e9f:43630dd1626245c2.summary: In a pre-registered hiring experiment (N=2, 680) embedded in a real tutor-hiring process, we investigate how student evaluators rate two fixed teaching samples submitted by two tutor applicants, one female- and one male-authored. We randomize whether the tutor applicants' gender pronouns are visible, whether ratings determine a real hire, and whether student evaluators are rewarded for matching the ratings of a gender-blind expert committee. Because only the pronoun is edited, differences in the rating gap between the two samples across pronoun conditions identify the effect of observable gender without requiring equally good samples. Contrary to the usual expectation of bias against women, making the two applicants' gender observable induces a reverse bias: it shifts the female-minus-male rating gap toward the female applicant and lowers the probability that evaluators choose the male applicant in a hypothetical hiring decision. Neither removing hiring consequences for the applicant nor rewarding student evaluators for matching expert ratings significantly changes this bias. The reversal is not a uniform shift toward the female applicant. It is concentrated among evaluators who state that women explain Microeconomics better, whereas evaluators who see no gender difference show no significant shift. Stated beliefs predict the rating gap only when applicant gender is visible.

59ec699e9f:3e655f8749a4262e.title: Fathersâ€™ Housework Participation and the Intergenerational Association in Housework Division: Evidence from Japan
59ec699e9f:3e655f8749a4262e.author: Chu Zhang
59ec699e9f:3e655f8749a4262e.summary: Routine housework remains strongly gendered in Japan despite the spread of dual-earner households. This study examines whether fathersâ€™ housework participation when respondents were aged 15 is associated with the division of housework in respondentsâ€™ later marital households. Using the Japanese Life Course Panel Survey, the analysis indicates that paternal housework participation is associated with a smaller female-to-male housework-frequency gap. Although the estimated association is larger for sons than for daughters, the difference is not statistically significant. The clearest estimated association is observed among sons whose mothers worked full-time, although formal evidence of cross-group differences remains limited. Supplementary analyses provide suggestive evidence that the association among sons is most clearly reflected in their own housework frequency and the shopping-specific gap, with weaker evidence for laundry, whereas the most precisely estimated result among daughters is less traditional gender-role attitudes toward housework. These patterns are consistent with different behavioral and attitudinal manifestations of intergenerational continuity, but they do not establish sex-specific mechanisms or causal effects.

59ec699e9f:e09c1f3a80027c7f.title: Place-Based Federal Procurement and Resident Jobs: Lessons from the Historically Underutilized Business Zone Program
59ec699e9f:e09c1f3a80027c7f.author: Craig Sylvera
59ec699e9f:e09c1f3a80027c7f.summary: Unlike tax-based place policies that subsidize employment or investment, procurement-based approaches direct federal purchasing to businesses in distressed areas. I examine the HUBZone program, which targets federal contracts to firms in economically disadvantaged census tracts. I find that receiving an award increases jobs for residents of the census tract by 3.5 percent over five to seven years, with no corresponding increase in jobs within the census tract. Establishment-level analysis reveals no employment gains at recipient firms themselves, suggesting any employment effects occur outside the receiving firm. Housing markets respond positively with increased mortgage origination activity. Examining the variation in the size of awards does not reveal a relationship between award size and jobs gained. The findings demonstrate that procurement set-asides can improve local outcomes in distressed areas, though whether they create new jobs or redistribute existing opportunities remains an open question.

59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.title: The Long-Term Mental Health Consequences of Emotional and Interpersonal Work Demands
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.author: Vincent Vandenberghe
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.summary: This paper examines how career-long emotional/interpersonal work demands are associated with mental health among adults aged 50 and older. Using retrospective work histories from SHARE combined with ISCO-4-level occupational characteristics from O*NET, we construct employment trajectories capturing cumulative exposure to emotionally/interpersonally demanding work and examine its association with later-life depressive symptoms, measured by the EURO-D scale. Our findings show that careerlong emotional/interpersonal demands are associated with a higher risk of depression after age 50, although their relative importance is modest. Career instability, such as employment gaps, redundancies, and part-time work, emerges as a stronger predictor. Pre-labour-market factors, including childhood health and educational attainment, also play a substantial role, highlighting the lasting importance of early-life circumstances for later-life mental health.

59ec699e9f:18406bc4f42407f6.title: A Macroeconomic Model of Ph.D. Enrollment with Income Risk and Non-Pecuniary Preferences
59ec699e9f:18406bc4f42407f6.author: Airi Hayama
59ec699e9f:18406bc4f42407f6.summary: Japan is expanding doctoral financial aid amid declining Ph.D. enrollment; Models Ph.D. enrollment decisions with heterogeneous â€œacademic tasteâ€ ; Heterogeneity in â€œacademic tasteâ€ drives Ph.D. enrollment decisions; Ignoring this heterogeneity overestimates the effects of financial aid; At equal cost, financial aid raises enrollment more; income insurance raises welfare more

59ec699e9f:8c95c14ec32882b9.title: The Fruits of Horticulture? Commercial Farming Across Local Economies in Senegal
59ec699e9f:8c95c14ec32882b9.author: Dieye, Mohamadou
59ec699e9f:8c95c14ec32882b9.summary: Can commercial farming stimulate economic development? Across sub-Saharan Africa, large commercial farms are increasingly promoted as engines of rural transformation. Yet whether they generate gains beyond the farm, and how these vary with local conditions, remains unclear. We construct a new spatial census tracing the expansion of large commercial farms in Senegal from 1999 to 2023 and combine it with satellite data, a farm survey, and population censuses. Local economic responses differ substantially across the four settings in which farms operate. In two horticultural regions with investments of similar scale and labor demand, census comparisons show increases in the share of women’s employment in agriculture. Near major urban markets, where commercial farms replace smallholder production, farm expansion increases nighttime-light coverage and is associated with higher household wealth and in-migration. In the less densely populated river valley, where farms expand cultivated land, census estimates point to population growth, but we find no comparable nighttime-light response and weaker evidence of rising wealth. In the other two settings, we find little evidence of local economic change.

59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.title: The Great Household Divergence - Economic Inequality and the Roots of Social Fracture for the 99%
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.author: Andrews, N. O.
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.summary: For decades, the debate over American inequality has centered on a single question: how unequal has the United States become? Increasingly, the more important question is different: does it matter that some Americans are pulling dramatically away from everyone else, even as real income rises for most people? This paper argues that the United States has undergone a Great Household Divergence: four decades of extraordinary prosperity coinciding with widening disparities in household market position â€” disparities that shape employment, status, dignity, health, and neighborhood opportunity. Economic distance has become social distance, accompanied by rising polarization and democratic strain. Mobility eroded for large segments of the population, leaving some American communities with world-class opportunity while others resemble the developing world. This paper weaves together literatures on inequality, mobility, polarization and social policy. It argues that the prevailing policy model has focused too heavily on correcting market outcomes after the fact, and points upstream toward pre-distribution policies that shape wages, collective bargaining, state-level employment institutions and macroeconomic conditions aimed at tighter labor markets. The central implication is that social cohesion in the U.S. cannot be restored through post-tax redistribution alone. Addressing inequality is more than the simple arithmetic of redistribution; it also requires attention to social cohesion, the earning power of Americans and human dignity.

59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.title: Which types of education raise firm productivity? Evidence for managers and workers in the UK
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.author: Hall, Tessa
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.summary: This paper estimates the firm productivity returns to degree field, institution quality, and degree level, and compares them with wage returns. I link a LinkedIn panel from Revelio Labs to Orbis financial accounts for over 20, 000 UK firms over 2015?2024. Within firms, a bachelor's degree raises a worker's productivity by around 20%; a top-20 institution adds a further 10% and a postgraduate qualification 6%. The returns differ by organisational role. A bachelor's degree raises productivity for managers and non-managers alike. Specialist credentials - a STEM field, an elite institution - raise productivity for non-managers but not for managers, whose premium loads instead on postgraduate qualifications, above all MBAs. Managers also contribute around 26% more than otherwise identical non-managers, a premium that education does not explain. Averaged over the workforce, wage premia are close to productivity premia for each type of degree. However, the average conceals two wedges of opposite sign: STEM-trained non-managers are paid below their relative productivity, and degree-holding managers above it. Finally, for a subset of firms matched to the World Management Survey, workforce education accounts for around a quarter the well-documented correlation between management practices and productivity.

59ec699e9f:8b4284d3c4b80277.title: The Dynamics of Rent-Sharing across Occupations
59ec699e9f:8b4284d3c4b80277.author: , Matteo
59ec699e9f:8b4284d3c4b80277.summary: We study how firm-level productivity gains are shared across the occupational hierarchy. Using Portuguese matched employer-employee data linked to firm balance sheets (2004–2019), we develop an algorithm that identifies permanent shocks to firm value added and estimate occupation-specific rent-sharing elasticities in an event-study design. Pass-through declines steeply along the job ladder: the elasticity of pay premia to value added per worker is about 0.20 for managers and supervisors, 0.11 for qualified workers, and 0.06 for low-qualified workers. This gap has widened over time, increasing within-firm inequality, as pass-through to low-qualified workers has halved. This decline is consistent with de-unionization, while we show that minimum wage increases do not crowd out rent sharing at the bottom. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.author: Hellsten, Mark
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.author: Xu, Yaling
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.author: Xiaoqing Zhou
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.summary: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.title: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.author: Camilo Morales-Jimenez
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.summary: The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.title: Do Pension Reforms Affect Migrants Differently? Evidence from Germany and Spain
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.author: Hao Wei
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.summary: This paper examines whether migrants and native-born workers respond differently to pension reforms that encourage longer working lives. Using longitudinal data from SHARE Waves 4â€“9 for Germany and Spain, we construct individual reform exposure based on country-specific reform timing, birth-cohort eligibility, and proximity to retirement age, and estimate models with individual and survey-wave fixed effects. Reform exposure is associated with a lower probability of retirement, with suggestive evidence of an additional decline among migrants. This migrant differential is particularly pronounced in Spain, while the corresponding estimate is small and statistically insignificant in Germany, although formal cross-country tests do not establish a statistically significant difference between the two countries. Complementary analyses indicate that adjustment is concentrated around retirement ages rather than reflecting a broad increase in employment, while evidence for effects on mental health and generalized trust is limited. Overall, the findings suggest that migrants may respond differently to pension reform, but that these differences are concentrated at specific retirement margins and depend on the institutional context

59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.title: Exploitation Cycles: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics in Labor Markets with Predatory Employers
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.author: Rusch, Hannes
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.summary: Exploitative employers damage the very labor force on which they depend. Accordingly, this paper models exploitation and labor-force quality as a coupled dynamical system: exploiters spread when high-quality labor makes extraction profitable, but their success degrades the labor environment that sustains those profits. We show that this coupling generates persistent cycles rather than convergence toastable level of exploitation. Our policy extension shows that responsive enforcement can dampen these cycles, induce convergence, and improve welfare. We contribute by elucidating exploitation dynamics and demonstrating how eco-evolutionary methods can be applied to study labor markets on which employers compete with exploiters.

4a32a2255e:72baa7219628dfb4.title: Strategic vision of regional development policy: Short-term and mid-term recommendations for Ukraine’s alignment with Chapter 22 of the EU acquis
4a32a2255e:72baa7219628dfb4.author: Ambre Maucorps
4a32a2255e:72baa7219628dfb4.summary: The report outlines the stakes and opportunities for Ukraine to achieve EU accession and post-war reconstruction simultaneously, focusing on regional development and territorial cohesion. In short, it lays out a strategic vision for Ukraine’s regional development policy that goes beyond mere administrative reform and addresses core issues of territorial equity, economic recovery, and national security. In doing so, the paper tackles fundamental questions of policy instruments tailored to differentiated territorial realities, capacities of local communities, coordination of policy interventions, and stable financing. It argues that Ukrainian policymakers involved in the design, implementation, and monitoring of an EU-compatible, crisis-resilient regional development policy will have to home in on institutional quality, capacity-building, strong and sustainable financing mechanisms, asymmetric devolution, multi-level coordination, citizen involvement, and evidence-based policymaking.

4a32a2255e:2cb08141edb7466e.title: Are Europe's cities too small? a Europe-USA comparison of the role of urban size in productivity and growth
4a32a2255e:2cb08141edb7466e.author: Storper, Michael
4a32a2255e:2cb08141edb7466e.summary: Europe's per capita income has fallen markedly behind that of the United States since the mid-2000s. This paper examines one overlooked dimension of the gap: the structure of urban systems. Using harmonized OECD data on Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) for 162 US and nearly 300 EU+UK urban areas over 2002-2023, we show that the US urban system follows Zipf's law (rank-size slope of -1.0). The European system is significantly flatter (-0.8). Europe lacks a group of large, highly productive second-rank metropolitan areas, which harbor over a quarter of US output. Productivity rises with city size on both continents, with pooled elasticities of about 0.10 in the US and 0.08 in Europe. At any given size, however, US cities are 15-25% more productive, and the gap widens above 5 million inhabitants, which comprises most of the numerous second tier cites in the US system. The US also allocates a much larger share of employment to its most productive cities (62% versus 36% in the top 50 productive FUAs). A simple compositional counterfactual suggests that adopting the US allocation would raise EU+UK GDP by about 11%. Moreover, while in 2008 the two FUA productivity distributions were similar, by 2021, they had diverged considerably. The US distribution shifted uniformly to the right, while the European distribution stagnated outside its converging lower tail. allocation gap is persistent, and so could help explain Europe's productivity deficit, it does not explain the post-2008 widening. Patent data point to larger and more frontier-oriented innovation hubs in US second-tier cities, a possible source of their unusually high contribution to US urban productivity. The purpose of this paper is to encourage further attention to the role of spatial structure in European economic performance.

4a32a2255e:a1274499d9d86cd1.title: Place-Based Federal Procurement and Resident Jobs: Lessons from the Historically Underutilized Business Zone Program
4a32a2255e:a1274499d9d86cd1.author: Craig Sylvera
4a32a2255e:a1274499d9d86cd1.summary: Unlike tax-based place policies that subsidize employment or investment, procurement-based approaches direct federal purchasing to businesses in distressed areas. I examine the HUBZone program, which targets federal contracts to firms in economically disadvantaged census tracts. I find that receiving an award increases jobs for residents of the census tract by 3.5 percent over five to seven years, with no corresponding increase in jobs within the census tract. Establishment-level analysis reveals no employment gains at recipient firms themselves, suggesting any employment effects occur outside the receiving firm. Housing markets respond positively with increased mortgage origination activity. Examining the variation in the size of awards does not reveal a relationship between award size and jobs gained. The findings demonstrate that procurement set-asides can improve local outcomes in distressed areas, though whether they create new jobs or redistribute existing opportunities remains an open question.

4a32a2255e:ebacb2402b0b8898.title: People, places and firms: improving our understanding of wage and productivity disparities
4a32a2255e:ebacb2402b0b8898.author: Overman, Henry G.
4a32a2255e:ebacb2402b0b8898.summary: In many countries spatial disparities in wages and productivity are large and persistent. This raises questions about the causes and consequences of such disparities. Two inter-related issues – the sorting of high skilled workers and the productivity benefits of urban density – are central to the way in which urban economists have approached these questions. In this commentary, we argue that despite the emerging consensus that sorting matters for wage disparities, the literature has made less progress on other dimensions of these disparities and a number of methodological issues remain unresolved.

4a32a2255e:7558cd5b236fa8d8.title: Tracing Climate Risk Knowledge from Local Priorities to Adaptation Visions: Linking Hazard Evidence and Socioeconomic Vulnerability across Eight European Metropolitan Regions
4a32a2255e:7558cd5b236fa8d8.author: Phoebe Koundouri
4a32a2255e:7558cd5b236fa8d8.summary: Climate risk depends not only on hazard intensity but also on exposure and on the capacity of societies to anticipate, absorb, adapt to and transform in response to climate shocks and stresses. Yet how socioeconomic vulnerability shapes the translation of locally salient hazards into adaptation priorities remains poorly understood, particularly in metropolitan regions with contrasting institutional capacities. We trace how climate-risk knowledge evolved in the eight metropolitan case study areas of the Horizon Europe CARMINE project: Athens, Barcelona, Birmingham, Bologna, Brasov, Funen-Odense, Leipzig and Prague. The pathway moves from local risk articulation in Living Lab workshops, through observed hazard characterisation, to socioeconomic contextualisation and stakeholder-developed 2050 adaptation visions. A socioeconomic vulnerability index combining sensitivity with structural resilience capacities (institutions, health, labour markets, skills, innovation and economic resources) is computed for 1, 499 European regions at the third level of the Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics and analysed for spatial autocorrelation. Vulnerability is strongly clustered, with hotspots in south-eastern Europe and the Mediterranean south. Athens and Brasov lie within the south-eastern hotspot, Funen-Odense in a coldspot and the remaining areas in transitional positions. Relating priority hazards to the most relevant vulnerability pillars, we classify the focal-hazard configurations as compounded in Athens, Barcelona, Bologna and Brasov, latent in Prague and managed in Funen-Odense and Leipzig. Similar hazards thus constitute different adaptation problems depending on the vulnerability context; in Barcelona and Bologna, compounded risk stems from weak institutions rather than social sensitivity. The hazard and vulnerability evidence confirmed, qualified or broadened locally articulated priorities. We draw implications for multi-level adaptation governance, for…

4a32a2255e:05a89cbc369c7772.title: From Reagan to Trump: regional development traps and the remaking of American electoral politics
4a32a2255e:05a89cbc369c7772.author: Glisson, Ali
4a32a2255e:05a89cbc369c7772.summary: This paper examines the territorial reconfiguration of American electoral politics since the 1980s, tracing the remaking of Republican support from Reagan’s 1984 landslide to Trump’s three presidential campaigns (2016, 2020, 2024). Drawing on panel data for every presidential election from 1984 to 2024 across 722 commuting zones, we test whether regional development traps, defined as enduring economic underperformance, explain both the shift from Democrats to Republicans and the Republicans’ internal realignment. Mundlak/Correlated Random Effects estimates show backlash is overwhelmingly driven by structural, not cyclical, decline. Short-term economic fluctuations do not predict Republican swing, while long-run territorial position does so decisively. Voters are not responding to recessions. They are registering alienation from an economic order that has failed their communities for a generation. Trump’s gains concentrated in places persistently left behind, whose peripheral position has become entrenched.

4a32a2255e:d7a9ea21e14a7ce2.title: Business networks and the persistence of entrepreneurship: evidence from China
4a32a2255e:d7a9ea21e14a7ce2.author: Lee, Neil
4a32a2255e:d7a9ea21e14a7ce2.summary: This paper investigates the long run association between business networks and entrepreneurship and regional development in China. We focus on chambers of commerce, bodies which facilitated networking between businesses until private firms were banned by Mao. Our results suggest that the pre-Mao chamber system is associated with long-lasting patterns of business creation and economic output in China, with this influence surviving until the post-1978 return of the market economy. The associations are strongest in the early reform period but weaken over time. We show evidence that historic chambers density is correlated with later social capital, despite major political change.

4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.title: Anchor or sinker – Large firms, anchoring capacity and regional development
4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.author: Nilsson, Magnus
4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.summary: This paper ties together two literatures which explain regional anchoring from different perspectives. One is based on the role of large organizations in anchoring an industry in a region, the other is systemic and deals with anchoring processes that circulate and embed knowledge. Each leaves implicit what the other explains. The aim is to understand how anchor effects and regional anchoring capacity interact across different regional contexts. Illustrative cases from three Swedish regions show how the two both diverge from and reinforce each other, anchor without anchoring and anchoring without an anchor, depending on regional configuration and anchor control.

4a32a2255e:8fbc98ed042d122e.title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
4a32a2255e:8fbc98ed042d122e.author: Chen, Ruoyu
4a32a2255e:8fbc98ed042d122e.summary: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources – OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land – by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.title: Multi-View Representation Learning for Regional Opportunity Spaces and Industrial Path Development
4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.author: Grillitsch, Markus
4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.summary: Regional opportunities for industrial development arise when local conditions favor particular economic activities. These conditions depend in part on a region’s existing industry profile and on the economic relationships among its activities. Heterogeneous data sources on mobility, production, and firm ownership provide complementary evidence about this underlying industrial structure. We therefore develop a multi-view representation-learning framework for industries that integrates these different sources into a shared latent representation. By using graph diffusion, the framework captures both direct and indirect connections between industries. Applied to Swedish industries over three decades and three classification versions, the learned representation places industries from different classification periods within a common latent space. To evaluate this operationalization of opportunity, we construct an opportunity-density measure by combining latent similarity with local industry size. Higher opportunity density is consistently associated with industry entry and startup formation and with lower industry exit. Across classification periods, a one-standard-deviation increase in opportunity density is associated with 5.3–6.2 percentage-point higher industry-entry probabilities (118–136% of baseline rates), 8.9–13.8 percentage-point lower industry-exit probabilities (147–209%), and 1.1–1.7 percentage-point higher startup-formation probabilities (131–187%). Opportunity density remains associated with these outcomes in 41 of 42 models after accounting for information contained in the individual data sources. Our machine-learning framework shows how heterogeneous data can be integrated into a common latent structure and used to operationalize regional opportunity spaces, providing a new approach to studying industrial path development.

33e1d7779a:9d7e33a04feb3afc.title: The pros and cons of Medicare for All
33e1d7779a:9d7e33a04feb3afc.author: David Nather
33e1d7779a:9d7e33a04feb3afc.summary: The boldest idea in health care comes down to one massive tradeoff: Guaranteed coverage for everyone in exchange for an eye-popping price tag and an ultra-messy transition. Why it matters: Talk of Medicare for All is growing now that Democrats will control Congress next year with huge majorities in both chambers — so it's time to take a clinical look at the pros and cons, based on what we're hearing from policy experts who have studied it. Driving the news: The idea is getting a fresh round of attention after Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) — a major supporter of Medicare for All who wrote a book about it — offered to name the plan "TrumpCare," complete with gold insurance cards, if President Trump helps pass it. Trump reposted his offer and has offered to meet with El-Sayed, telling the New York Post : "Maybe there's some place in the middle that we could go." Reality check: They will probably meet, and it could end with mutual praise and hopeful vibes (with echoes of Trump's meetings with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani). El-Sayed likes to flatter Trump. Trump likes to be flattered. But don't take that as a sign that a deal is imminent. There's pretty much zero common ground, other than calling it TrumpCare. Trump hates Medicare for All . Trump is all about cutting more drug price deals and sending people money to buy their own coverage — hardly a big government takeover of the health system. But Democrats can certainly try to force votes on Medicare for All when they're in power, although they're likely to find that not everyone in the party is on board. Medicare for All backers are wagering that enough people are fed up with the existing health system that they'll accept a bigger federal role providing coverage to more Americans, warts and all. "It's no longer [enough] from a political policy point of view to tinker around the edges," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) told reporters last week. "Increasingly, elected officials understand the current health care…

33e1d7779a:277780eb5a68c4df.title: Cookbook GPT: When AI becomes a Thanksgiving sous-chef
33e1d7779a:277780eb5a68c4df.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:277780eb5a68c4df.summary: From cookbooks to YouTube to ChatGPT , the way Americans plan their holiday menus has evolved. The big picture: But there's something uniquely human about building a recipe, and chefs warn we risk fracturing personal connections and family history by reducing culinary traditions to chatbot prompts. "Recipes can have tradition and ritual," says Melanie Underwood, a culinary educator and founder of Nourish & Gather . She warns that taking the human conversation out of cooking could further erode our cultural oral histories. Context: Campbell's recent State of the Sides survey found that 27% of U.S. adults who celebrate Thanksgiving have used generative AI for holiday planning or cooking, up from 22% last year. And 65% of shoppers say they would like to use AI in some aspect of holiday meal planning, per holiday shopper trend research from FMI, the Food Industry Association. Among those celebrating at least one holiday this season, 34% say they'd use AI to find new recipes, 23% said they'd use it to plan the overall menu and 16% said they'd use it to make the holiday meal healthier. Friction point: Food bloggers and chefs have warned that traffic to their trusted websites is plummeting with the rise of AI recipe summaries, forcing some to quit the game altogether. Plus, AI recipes on the " slop "-pier side can be disastrous for the dinner table. The AI-generated recipes that pop up on Google's search results page "are often total nonsense," recipe blogger Eb Gargano told Axios in an email. "They've been generated by AI – and, at least last time I checked – AI cannot cook a recipe or taste a recipe," she said. Food bloggers have a name for those recipes, she added: "Frankenstein recipes." Underwood says she uses AI to help her with the operational side of her business. But when she recently asked a chatbot to scale her recipe for a large event and make a shopping list, it cut out ingredients — saying it was trying to improve her recipe. Our thought bubble: AI is not a…

33e1d7779a:aae33c1cefefabc9.title: Musk makes $18 billion SpaceX stock pledge for every kid in America
33e1d7779a:aae33c1cefefabc9.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:aae33c1cefefabc9.summary: Elon Musk on Wednesday pledged two SpaceX shares for every child in America, doubling an offer he made just last month. Why it matters: The $18 billion-plus giveaway roughly triples Michael Dell's once record-breaking Trump accounts gift . What they're saying: " Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," he said in a post to X. On Oct. 19, he promised that every child would receive one share next year, adding it would be the "first of many."
