By the numbers: With about 72 million minors in the U.S. per Census estimates, and at SpaceX's closing price Wednesday, the gift would be worth around $18.35 billion. Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares, and the company has billions of shares outstanding, so the giveaway likely wouldn't have much impact on him or investors. Yes, but: The stock's fallen about 13% since he made the initial promise, amid a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks. Zoom in: Musk's pledge isn't the first from SpaceX. In July the company's COO Gwynne Shotwell said she'd gift a share of the stock to each of 2 million Trump accounts. What's next: Musk did not offer a timing for the new distribution.

33e1d7779a:76cbbc41981061bf.title: Macy's Thanksgiving parade postponed for the first time in the event's history
33e1d7779a:76cbbc41981061bf.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:76cbbc41981061bf.summary: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in the event's history, the retailer confirmed Wednesday. Why it matters: Macy's was expected to celebrate its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade with a record 100 inflatables — but an impending nor'easter will keep its iconic giant balloons from flying on the holiday. What they're saying: "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's told NBC on Wednesday. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year," Macy's said. The parade has been pushed back to Saturday. NBC will air last year's parade during the allocated Thanksgiving time slot. What we're watching: It's unclear if any scheduled performers will be unable to participate following the postponement, but thousands are involved in the parade each year. Saturday's forecast currently shows mostly sunny conditions and a high of 55 degrees, according to the National Weather Service . Driving the news: A large storm bringing mostly rain and wind to the East Coast could disrupt travel plans, holiday parades and more this Thanksgiving, per projections from AccuWeather. High winds could also cause widespread sporadic power outages across the region, disrupting holiday meal preparations. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning for Manhattan on Wednesday morning, with sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts of up to 55 mph forecast for Thursday. How it works: Large balloons can't fly when sustained winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts exceed 34 mph, per rules announced by former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani in 1998. The NYPD has ultimate authority over whether balloons should fly. Worth noting: The parade set an all-time viewership record in 2025, with an estimated 34.3 million people watching across NBC and the…

33e1d7779a:a8b01bc4ee4c28ee.title: "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter": Democrats demand new restrictions on AI
33e1d7779a:a8b01bc4ee4c28ee.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:a8b01bc4ee4c28ee.summary: Prominent Democrats are calling for new restrictions on AI development following Axios reporting that employees at OpenAI and Anthropic increasingly fear their most powerful models cannot be safely released. Why it matters: The political debate over AI is expanding beyond the economic consequences of the technology to a more existential question: whether companies should be allowed to build systems they may not be able to control. The issue is gaining traction among Democratic leaders ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.), a potential 2028 contender, outlined a playbook for AI regulations in an interview with "The Axios Show," noting that voters hate the technology because they fear losing control . Driving the news: Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for immediate action: "The people inside AI companies are sounding the alarm ," Kelly said. "We built protections for nuclear weapons and other dangerous technologies, so why are we waiting with AI? We need safeguards and independent examiners in these companies, now." "It is absolutely indefensible to say 'we will take this up next year' when the risks are imminent and the alarm is nearly universal," Schatz said. "The flashing red lights couldn't be brighter, and yet big tech refuses stop," Van Hollen said. "Inaction is not an option. Congress must step up." Sanders went further, calling for a halt to advanced AI development : "The humans who are creating AI fear it could soon escape their own control," Sanders said. "Congress must act and pause advanced AI development NOW." Catch up quick: More than two dozen sources familiar with internal debates at OpenAI and Anthropic told Axios that recent breakthroughs in AI capabilities have raised questions about whether future frontier models can be safely released. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some…

33e1d7779a:46ac3b65de55fff5.title: Anthropic CEO pushes back on Axios reporting on AI and free will
33e1d7779a:46ac3b65de55fff5.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:46ac3b65de55fff5.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Wednesday rejected the notion that humans should surrender free will to AI, pushing back on Axios' reporting about a growing ideological divide among top AI executives. Why it matters: This is Amodei's most significant public remarks since the company went public last week. What he's saying: "We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei said. Amodei distinguished between handing over governance to AI, which he opposes, and automating specific tasks, on which he holds more nuanced views. He said his view is mixed on specific instances like "AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end" where "it is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives" if AI systems are allowed more agency. He also said it may make sense to slow or stop certain AI deployments to mitigate job disruption and limit AI's ability to autonomously develop more powerful systems. The big picture: The debate about control comes amid a rocky debut for Anthropic's stock, which dipped below its IPO day price on Wednesday. The intrigue: Amodei also took aim at rival AI executives, accusing them of engaging in "vibes-based commercial and political positioning" by championing human agency without meaningfully differentiating their products. Those executives, he said, "repeat slogans like 'human control and agency,' or 'AI should be just a tool,' without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans."

33e1d7779a:9f3c068b5d476f18.title: Scoop: Kushner urges Netanyahu to make good on Gaza commitments
33e1d7779a:9f3c068b5d476f18.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:9f3c068b5d476f18.summary: Presidential envoy Jared Kushner urged Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday to make good on commitments he made to Donald Trump to implement a Gaza peace plan , according to three sources with knowledge of a call between them. Why it matters: The White House and Trump's Board of Peace have been increasingly exasperated by what they viewed as Netanyahu's obstinacy on Gaza, convinced that he's been prioritizing his political survival above all else. "I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status," Kushner said in a New York Magazine interview published Monday. But two sources with knowledge of the call said it was "positive and constructive." One of them said Netanyahu signaled again that he's ready to move forward with the steps in Gaza that the White House wants. A third source confirmed that Netanyahu said he's committed to the Gaza plan. The Israeli prime minister's office confirmed that the call took place but declined to comment further. The big picture: The Gaza roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election and now wants the prime minister to reciprocate. But many of the Gaza measures are loathed by Netanyahu's base. Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, currently has a window to form a new government. He's making progress, and if he succeeds, Netanyahu could be ousted as early as next week. Eisenkot promised during the campaign to implement Trump's Gaza plan with the goal of ensuring that Hamas no longer controls the territory within 18 months. Catch up quick: In July, the Board of Peace agreed with…

33e1d7779a:0433be7d492bf361.title: The U.S. economy is ripping
33e1d7779a:0433be7d492bf361.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:0433be7d492bf361.summary: Wall Street has been reeling amid fears about the future of the AI boom. But in the here and now, the U.S. economy is experiencing an outright boom. The big picture: Growth was even stronger this summer than it appeared, and the robust expansion is continuing this fall, according to a range of data released Wednesday morning. That is pushing Americans' incomes up and the pace of layoffs down. The strong data helps explain why the Federal Reserve is prepared to raise interest rates two weeks from now even in the face of financial market turbulence. Driving the news: The U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the second revision to GDP data — well above the 3.4% originally reported. The strong results have continued into Q4. The Commerce Department separately said that personal income rose 0.7% in October, well ahead of analysts' expectations. Overall orders for durable goods came in below forecasts for October, but core capital goods orders — a forward-looking measure of investment spending — climbed 1.2%, also well ahead of projections. The Labor Department said that only 189,000 people filed new claims for jobless benefits last week, matching the lowest of 2026 and among the lowest readings on record (claims go back to 1967). Zoom out: The Q3 GDP reading was powered by business investment, especially for software, showing that the AI buildout remains a powerful driver of overall economic growth. It wasn't driven by volatile components of GDP like inventory and trade swings; real final sales to private domestic purchasers surged at a whopping 5.8% pace, and gross domestic income — conceptually similar to GDP — rose at a 4.4% rate. Translation: This isn't some fluky reading, but rather a sign of underlying robustness. Rapid growth looks set to continue in Q4; the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tool estimates current-quarter growth at 2.9%. Zoom in: Nonresidential fixed investment — the GDP subcategory that covers capital…

33e1d7779a:6577f5c564b3f507.title: Army detonates Iowa explosives amid toxic lead fears
33e1d7779a:6577f5c564b3f507.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:6577f5c564b3f507.summary: The Army detonated 68 drums of unstable lead azide on an Iowa plant Wednesday after multiple delays, a court challenge and presidential intervention . The big picture: Elected officials slammed the military over communication shortfalls ahead of the detonation, which triggered evacuations, closures and fears about exposure to toxic lead dust in surrounding communities and states . Federal officials have repeatedly stressed that detonating the unstable lead is safer than risking it exploding spontaneously. What they're saying: "Early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations," President Trump said on Truth Social . Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe also said early analysis from federal partners indicates the detonation was "well-contained." The Army has not yet released a statement on the status of the operation. Reporters near the plant witnessed large clouds of smoke rising following the detonation. Context: The evacuation zone is a 5-mile cone extending southwest of the ammunition plant, per the Army's public safety notice . Evacuees are set to receive notice by phone when it's safe to return. Those outside of the evacuation zone should still shelter in place by closing all windows and doors, recirculating heating and turning off fans that pull in outside air, among other protective measures for children and livestock, per the Army. State of play: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate the explosives on Monday, saying the blast couldn't proceed without approval from a court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . But Trump warned he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. The court initially granted an administrative stay but lifted it Monday, allowing the plan to proceed. Sand said in a statement that the administration should decide "based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago…

33e1d7779a:90e8391ed309a5fa.title: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter
33e1d7779a:90e8391ed309a5fa.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:90e8391ed309a5fa.summary: Data: Bureau of Economic Analysis ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios The U.S. economy grew substantially faster this summer than initially thought, the government said Wednesday — a blockbuster upgrade to its estimate of third-quarter GDP. By the numbers: The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate, up from the 3.4% initially reported and nearly twice the rate of 2.2% in the second quarter. Why it matters: The economy has even more momentum than previously understood, a sign of remarkable resilience in the face of higher borrowing costs and stubborn inflation that could give the Fed more latitude to raise rates. Zoom in: The upward revision reflected stronger business investment fueled by the AI buildout and software investment, as well as consumer spending. A measure of underlying private-sector demand — which strips out trade, inventories and government spending — rose at a whopping 5.8% annual rate, up from the 4.9% initially reported. The backdrop: Separate data out Wednesday showed personal income jumped 0.7% in October while inflation-adjusted consumer spending stalled, pushing the saving rate up to 4.1% from 3.6% the prior month. The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — climbed 3.8% from a year earlier, from 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, accelerated to 3.3% from 3.1%. On a monthly basis, both headline and core prices rose 0.3%. The bottom line: The U.S. economy was on remarkably strong footing heading into the end of the year, though inflation remains stubbornly high. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

33e1d7779a:4abbf759f440252d.title: Trump prepares new round of tariffs on China, other U.S. trading partners
33e1d7779a:4abbf759f440252d.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:4abbf759f440252d.summary: The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity. Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns. Post-election polling indicates voters overwhelmingly want tariffs to stay at current levels or decline. There's relatively little support — even among Trump's base — for them rising. Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs largely target specific goods, a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed. China is the exception: The proposed 20% tariff would apply to most Chinese imports, with that rate calibrated to preserve the nations' trade truce. These new tariffs would not be added to existing ones aimed at combating forced labor or certain sector-specific tariffs, a senior U.S. official said. The official added that the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to live up to its commitments. Between the lines: The proposed tariff rates for other major trading partners are consistent with parameters set out in trade deals, the official said. Trade deals struck with the EU, Japan and South Korea last year established 15% tariff rates on most goods. Other economies targeted include Taiwan, India, Indonesia and Vietnam. On average, the proposals would raise existing tariff rates on targeted trading partners by roughly 5 percentage points, the official estimated. The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers. The proposed tariffs are subject to a public comment period and hearings, with the levies…

33e1d7779a:881d75b86058e98d.title: "The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting."
33e1d7779a:881d75b86058e98d.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:881d75b86058e98d.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D), a potential 2028 presidential contender, asserted in an interview with "The Axios Show" that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to AI because of billionaire greed and clout. He said voters hate the technology because they fear losing control. Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, told Mike Allen this week that after an " AI earthquake " helped propel Democrats to huge midterm gains, Congress must treat oversight of the technology as an "emergency" for the first 100 hours of Democratic control. Why it matters: Moore, 48, focused on AI early, with an executive order in 2024 . He has used his NGA leadership roles to work across the aisle on AI protections, arguing that Marylanders can't afford to wait for Washington and shouldn't have to wait for a disaster . Moore, Maryland's first Black governor , is a former Army paratrooper who deployed to combat in Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division, and was a Rhodes Scholar and White House fellow. What they're saying: Moore, speaking at the Maryland State House in Annapolis, makes it clear in this episode of "The Axios Show" that AI will be a huge focus of the 2028 presidential race after becoming a flashpoint in November's midterms. Among the governor's key points: On the pace of regulation: "We are watching a fast-moving technology that is being protected at a snail's pace." On why people hate AI: "Genesis 1 talks about how God gave humanity dominion over all land, air and sea. And that dominion was given to humanity, not to robots." On whether regulating AI lets China win: "This is not a question of U.S. versus China. This is a question of man versus machine." On a bubble: "We are in a bubble because you cannot have that much influence by such a small group of companies." On Nvidia and Trump: "It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee. ... We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves making this…

33e1d7779a:19584ccf5395796c.title: Most blame government for return of measles: Poll
33e1d7779a:19584ccf5395796c.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:19584ccf5395796c.summary: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans hold government leaders responsible for the loss of the United States' measles elimination status , according to a new Ipsos poll . But there are few signs that the public wants to dwell on it. Why it matters: Partisan divisions over vaccines and outbreaks are so entrenched that Democrats won't have a broad mandate beyond their base to investigate the government's response when they take control of Congress. There's also a generational divide. People age 65 and over — who remember the introduction of the measles vaccine — are more likely to say the current situation bothers them a lot. What they found: Roughly 3 in 5 Americans (58%) think the loss of the measles elimination status could have been prevented if government leaders had done a better job encouraging people to get vaccinated and responding to outbreaks. 38% said there wasn't much government leaders could have done, because people make their own health decisions. There's a huge partisan split behind those numbers: 84% of Democrats say the return of measles could have been avoided if the government had done a better job, compared with 38% of Republicans. Just over a quarter of Americans (26%) say they're extremely or very concerned about an outbreak occurring in their community. There's a nearly 30-percentage-point partisan gap on concern, with 42% of Democrats extremely or very concerned, compared with 13% of Republicans. Independents are in the middle (25%). The findings come as Americans are sharply divided over the prospect of the next Congress investigating the Trump administration. And if COVID-19 is any guide, the public tends to be eager to put public health calamities in the rearview. A Reuters-Ipsos post-election poll found that just 10% of Republicans said they want the new Congress to focus a great deal or quite a bit on investigating the Trump administration, compared with 71% of Democrats. "As frustrating as the loss of measles elimination status is for many…

33e1d7779a:0c66e6827e0c203b.title: GOP firm's executive linked to effort to oust Republican senators
33e1d7779a:0c66e6827e0c203b.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:0c66e6827e0c203b.summary: A top executive at one of the Republican Party's most influential consulting firms was involved in a multimillion-dollar effort to defeat two GOP senators — Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska — in the midterm elections, Axios has learned. The firm, Axiom Strategies, is widely seen as the GOP's biggest consulting operation, with deep ties to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and other prominent Republican figures. Why it matters: It's exceedingly rare — if not unprecedented — for an executive at a major political consulting firm to work for groups seeking to defeat senators from the firm's own party in a general election. Driving the news: Federal election records identify Thomas Datwyler, who was listed on Axiom's website as CEO of its AxCapital division, as treasurer and custodian of records for three super PACs that reported more than $9.9 million in spending that targeted Husted and Sullivan, who lost their bids for reelection. The three super PACs were registered between March and October. Axiom founder Jeff Roe learned of Datwyler's involvement from a lawyer on Oct. 30 and demanded his resignation, according to a source with knowledge of the situation. Datwyler resigned that day, and Axiom says it will finish unwinding its relationship with him by Dec. 31. He was removed from the company's website Tuesday. Roe also contacted the White House to inform officials of what he had discovered, the source said. Zoom out: The super PACs boosted lesser-known candidates, including Republicans and Libertarians, in apparent attempts to draw conservative votes away from Sullivan and Husted. It's unclear what impact the groups' work had on the senators' defeats. The groups ran digital ads attacking the senators from the right, accusing Sullivan of supporting gender-transition surgeries for children and Husted of backing gun control measures. Right for Alaska spent nearly $2.4 million through Sept. 30, while Alaska Values PAC reported at least $3.75 million in spending…

33e1d7779a:77a5f15eebf9d1ec.title: Trump faces looming wave of ICE lawsuits
33e1d7779a:77a5f15eebf9d1ec.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:77a5f15eebf9d1ec.summary: The Trump administration is facing the first of possibly hundreds of lawsuits testing whether it can be held liable for how immigration officers acted during the ICE crackdowns . Why it matters: These cases could force the administration to defend the conduct of officers operating under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and now-retired Border Patrol Commander-at-large Greg Bovino. Driving the news: Democracy Forward, an advocacy litigation nonprofit, filed its first Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) case on Monday on behalf of Dayanne Figueroa. Figueroa, a U.S. citizen, was arrested during Operation Midway Blitz in Chicago in October 2025. Video footage of Figueroa's arrest, after dropping her son off at school, shows officers driving into her vehicle and dragging her out of her car by her legs in a chaotic scene with multiple witnesses. Under FTCA, she could file for monetary compensation. And if the case goes to trial, discovery could reveal more information about the directives to make arrests during Operation Midway Blitz. What they're saying: "I anticipated that I was going to be met with silence. I'm not surprised, but again, I still expect accountability, so I'm not gonna let that define the outcome of all this," Figueroa said in an exclusive interview with Axios. "I want my experience to be a catalyst for meaningful change." Figueroa has also testified before Congress and filed a police report over her experience. She is now asking for no more than $1 million, according to the FTCA filing, which alleges unlawful arrest, battery and failure to provide medical care. Zoom in: Figueroa's claim comes after filing an administrative complaint against DHS over its officers' conduct both during her arrest and while she was detained. The administration had six months to respond, but didn't, opening her path to an FTCA case. "This is really a sort of tip of the spear of this type of case," Jeff Dubner, an attorney leading the effort for Democracy Forward,…

33e1d7779a:ace489d1ee3230b9.title: Rival AI leaders push back against Anthropic vision of surrendering human agency to AI
33e1d7779a:ace489d1ee3230b9.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:ace489d1ee3230b9.summary: Top AI executives are increasingly pushing back against a common view inside Anthropic: that humanity should surrender some decision-making power to superintelligent AI systems, sources told Axios. That would put us on a slippery slope to forfeiting free will, critics say. Why it matters : The debate has picked up steam as top AI companies develop models certain employees consider too powerful to ever release . Many see Anthropic as the first company that will confront these questions due to its lead at the frontier of AI development. While critics have yet to call out the company by name, their public defenses of human agency and control take direct aim at what some have come to see as the worldview of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. When AI systems far surpass human intelligence, Amodei has said repeatedly that it will be preferable to turn over decision-making for "life-critical" cases to AI, and also said AI should oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources. Flashback: A product vision slide from several years ago that was revealed during litigation described Anthropic's "vision for a better world" as a "utopia ruled by god in a box." The big picture: The thinking for Amodei and others is that once AI can demonstrably cure diseases, safeguard humans from harming themselves or prevent disasters better than any person, refusing to hand over control becomes irrational — or even unethical. Proponents point to self-driving cars to make their case: Once statistical evidence points to autonomous vehicles being safer than human drivers, it is logical for humans to drive far less, if at all, they say. Inside Anthropic, a broad consensus has developed among some employees that humanity will—and in many cases should — safely hand over authority to superintelligent systems rather than fighting to retain control, according to people familiar with internal discussions. An Anthropic spokesperson said Amodei has advocated for human control of AI in many public…

33e1d7779a:5e7b583accc3c68a.title: This Thanksgiving won't be stuffed with politics, Americans say: Poll
33e1d7779a:5e7b583accc3c68a.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:5e7b583accc3c68a.summary: Data: YouGov; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios. Note: Data for this question among 929 adults who say they're celebrating Thanksgiving After November's midterm blue wave , Democrats are more likely to say political discussions will be on the table this Thanksgiving than Republicans, per recent polling . Why it matters: The volatility and vitriol of modern politics often threatens to infiltrate our social dynamics. Still, most Americans doubt the holiday will bring political arguments. By the numbers: In YouGov's survey, 37% of respondents planning to celebrate Thanksgiving said they were at least somewhat likely to discuss politics during dinner. More than half (56%) say politics is not likely to come up during their gathering. Yes, but: The share who expect to talk politics this year varies by party affiliation. Forty-five percent of Democrats celebrating Thanksgiving say they expect political conversations, compared to 28% of Independents and 39% of Republicans in YouGov's trend. Zoom in: And more than eight in ten think politics won't start turkey day tiffs: Just 12% expect arguments over politics at the celebration. Those numbers are relatively stable among political ideologies: 83% of Democrats, 82% of Independents and 85% of Republicans aren't prepping for a political food fight this year. Last year, among all respondents in YouGov's poll , 11% expected arguments, compared to 72% who didn't. Zoom out: Data for Progress, a progressive polling and research organization, similarly found that 11% of likely voters said they'd definitely discuss politics at Thanksgiving, and 26% said they probably would. Another 59% said they probably or definitely would not. However, 65% said they plan to talk at least some about the cost of living. Friction point: Even if political arguments don't fuel Thanksgiving stress, pocketbook strain is another story. This year, the average Thanksgiving dinner is up 6%, ending three straight years of price declines, according to the American Farm…

33e1d7779a:5e855f7da76d185c.title: Trump talks turkey, and his ballroom, at pardoning event
33e1d7779a:5e855f7da76d185c.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:5e855f7da76d185c.summary: President Trump honored a time-worn Washington tradition Tuesday: pardoning poultry — after using the pulpit to praise his White House ballroom and deliver a rally-reminiscent speech. The big picture: Freedom and Feathers, this year's honored birds, continue a bizarre American tradition officially dating back to 1989 — but building on far older presidential lore. Driving the news: "Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodations to host such distinguished guests," Trump said at the event, held on the White House's South Lawn. He continued, "I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built." Trump's hotly contested project will be a 90,000-square-foot addition, far larger than the main White House. "I've heard better," he said about the birds' names, though they still earned presidential pardons. Both birds will dodge the oven and retire at Texas A&M University. State of play: The collective 82 pounds of white-feathered flamboyance traveled from West Virginia's Deans Gap Farm for the event. Pointing to his large 2024 election win in West Virginia, Trump said Tuesday, "I won it by a lot. I don't know what the hell happened with this last election. Somebody, please explain it to me." The pair are just four months old. Per a White House fact sheet , Freedom's favorite treat is Dr. Pepper. Feathers prefers to snack on Golden Delicious apples, which — like the turkeys — hail from West Virginia. Between the lines: Trump has never shied away from using the event to ruffle feathers. Last year, he jabbed at former President Biden and attacked Chicago leadership, derailing the focus on his feathered guests by calling Gov. JB Pritzker (D) a "fat slob." During his first term, he joked that the turkeys trotting before him had were slated to "appear in Adam Schiff's basement," a nod to the Democrat who led the 2019 impeachment inquiry into Trump. While Trump…

33e1d7779a:cd514e041eebc477.title: Criminal charge against incoming House Democrat dropped
33e1d7779a:cd514e041eebc477.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:cd514e041eebc477.summary: Prosecutors in Mecklenburg County, N.C., announced Tuesday they are dropping a criminal charge against Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) related to an un-returned rental car in 2019. Why it matters: The charge had been a bothersome footnote for Womack since her sudden rise from obscurity on Election Day, when she unexpectedly won a heavily Republican district. Womack, a 49-year-old minister and consultant, is one of several "wave babies" who were largely unknown to national Democrats before their upset midterm victories. Driving the news: Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather said in a statement released Tuesday afternoon that his office has submitted a voluntary dismissal and that the matter is "closed." Womack was charged with "Felony Failure to Return Hired Property" after failing to return a rental car in 2019 following two renewals, Merriweather said. The car was recovered by law enforcement. A criminal summons was issued against Womack in 2020 but only served on Oct. 11 of this year, just days before the start of early voting. Merriweather said that the unidentified rental dealer has reached an agreement with Womack, in which she paid them the "assessed rental cost" of the car from its overdue date to its return, and does "not wish to proceed further with prosecution and considered the matter resolved." What they're saying: " For almost seven years Ms. Womack was unaware a criminal summons had been issued," Womack's lawyer Harold Cogdell said in a statement shared with Axios. "Upon learning of this unresolved matter, Ms. Womack promptly and fully resolved this matter with the rental car company." Cogdell said there are "questions remaining" about the timing of the summons being served, but that "Ms. Womack's [sic] is laser focused on preparing to serve the residents of the North Carolina's 14th Congressional District." Womack, who has said she was experiencing housing insecurity in 2019, referred Axios to Cogdell's statement when sought…

33e1d7779a:c765cdd879b99a59.title: Oil's downward trend is pushing gasoline lower
33e1d7779a:c765cdd879b99a59.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:c765cdd879b99a59.summary: Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Brent crude is trading below $90 per barrel to start the week and briefly dipped to its lowest level since late August. Why it matters: Recent declines should help gasoline prices keep falling. The average U.S. retail price is $3.61 per gallon, down nearly 70 cents over the last month, per AAA data. The big picture: "The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz," ING analysts write. Catch up quick: Qatar's prime minister met with Vice President JD Vance at the White House on Monday to discuss talks with Iran, according to Axios' Barak Ravid. Reality check: Major risks remain, with the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region remaining a very dangerous place, so don't assume the downward trend will continue. And nothing is really back to normal. The market intelligence firm Kpler finds tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was 42% below prewar levels in the seven days through Nov. 21, the WSJ reports. Flashback: The International Energy Agency on Nov. 13 predicted the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter with supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict. The bottom line: "The status quo is growing ever more bearish," Sparta Commodities' Aaron Kildow said in a note Monday. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

33e1d7779a:3a6ff639d8f098f8.title: "The Axios Show": Bob Woodward's memoir spills 50 years of secrets
33e1d7779a:3a6ff639d8f098f8.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:3a6ff639d8f098f8.summary: Bob Woodward — out Tuesday with " Secrets ," his memoir of 55 years of reporting for The Washington Post and 24 cinematic bestsellers, covering 10 presidents — told me in an interview for "The Axios Show" that the book exposes some confidential sources who are now dead because he feels a duty to history. Why it matters: Woodward, 83, is a double Pulitzer winner whose Watergate investigative reporting with Carl Bernstein became a book and movie, "All the President's Men," that inspired generations of would-be reporters, including me. But no journalism school teaches students they can out " secret sources " who are dead, as Woodward does in " Secrets ." "It's history," Woodward told me in the Georgetown home where so many sources have spilled to him, administration after administration, decade after decade. He explained that in many cases, the sources were widely known anyway or appeared in other files and records that have become public. He said some living sources gave him permission to be named in the book. "Look at the histories that come out — the Adams-Jefferson letters , which were very secret. But when they come out, historians rejoice. We now see what they were saying to each other ... I'm for history on occasions like that." Axios: "So you have zero qualms?" Woodward: "Well, you always have qualms, but what's your responsibility to get the history right? ... [For] people who are reading the history and trying to understand it deeper into the story, deeper is naming those sources." More from our interview, which you can watch here: Axios: " Based on your reporting, and your rich understanding of governance, put President Trump's level of corruption in historical perspective. How does President Trump compare to Richard Nixon, the president you helped bring down?" Woodward: "Trump is worse, much worse than Nixon. And the evidence is on two fronts: First of all, how much money he's made — billions of dollars himself as president. I mean, imagine that. It used…

33e1d7779a:bbaebd671d876651.title: Behind the Curtain: When reality shouts
33e1d7779a:bbaebd671d876651.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:bbaebd671d876651.summary: We naturally assume people in business and power are slightly full of it, spinning us wildly to exaggerate their achievements or capabilities. In the case of AI and its ability to do irreparable damage to society, it's time for all of us — the media, the White House and Congress — to believe them: They've truly built something we don't understand and soon, if not already, can't fully control. Why it matters: This is no longer a future problem. It's a today problem, if not a crisis. You see this with near-daily glitches at airports or banks. You see this in our reporting about two dozen researchers inside these companies claiming their AI is too powerful and uncontrollable to release. And you see this in AI execs' own on-the-record warnings that we're at or near the point of the technology surpassing comprehension or control. Just believe them. If we wait for a cyberattack on the U.S. electricity grid or some bad actor to release a pathogen at an elementary school, it's too late. We'll panic and make rushed, emotional decisions and bad policies. It's not too late to prevent this, while still getting the upside benefits of AI. In our conversations with hundreds of people involved in building and regulating AI, there's shockingly wide agreement about the dangers ahead — and ways to protect against the worst outcomes. There's just no mechanism or urgency to bring the right mix of people together to do this. The steps seem clear: Make this a society-wide, urgent call to action. This should be an all-hands-on-deck moment, the only topic Congress prioritizes short-term. Yes, it probably requires presidential leadership, and Trump is reluctant to slow things down. But his top cyber officials privately agree with us: This demands fast, smart, bipartisan action with heavy private sector involvement. Let 'er rip no longer feels like a plausible plan. Focus on safety and cyber first. Most leading AI companies would gladly slow down a bit, prioritize verifiable safety…

33e1d7779a:f5aad627bf950532.title: Scoop: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models are too unsafe to release
33e1d7779a:f5aad627bf950532.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:f5aad627bf950532.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates. Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen , sources told Axios. Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely. Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers. The rapid advances in reasoning across domains including math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have also made the models difficult, if not impossible, to contain or control in internal tests, the sources said. Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said. This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. Debate has also centered around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios. What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us…they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios. "And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we've had at work up until now sort of go out the…

33e1d7779a:470a591a786396c1.title: Scoop: ACLU eyes Supreme Court flips in 11 states
33e1d7779a:470a591a786396c1.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:470a591a786396c1.summary: The American Civil Liberties Union is expanding its state Supreme Court election fight into deep-red territory after the midterms left Texas just one judicial seat away from a Democratic majority, the group tells Axios. Why it matters: The next battles over abortion, voting rights, redistricting, religion in schools and LGBTQ protections could hinge on state Supreme Court races often overshadowed by federal campaigns. Those courts have become increasingly important arbiters of constitutional rights as the U.S. Supreme Court has given states greater latitude to set their own policies. By the numbers: The ACLU now eyes Supreme Court races in 11 states in 2027 and 2028, the group's chief political and advocacy officer Deirdre Schifeling tells Axios. The ACLU worked on court elections in five states this year. It spent $30 million on its broader electoral program, with Supreme Court races claiming the biggest share, she says. The group says it contacted 8 million voters through mail, digital ads, phone banks, door knocking and other outreach, according to the organization. Zoom in: Texas shows how fast a court can swing. Democrats swept all four Supreme Court races this month, winning seats on the state's highest civil court for the first time since 1994. Once the winners take office, Republicans' 9-0 majority will shrink to 5-4. Democrats need to flip just one of three Republican-held seats on the 2028 ballot to take control. The court unanimously vacated a lower-court order in 2024 that would have widened access to medical exceptions under the state's abortion restrictions. " That's a gigantic shift in one election cycle," Schifeling tells Axios. Zoom out: Democrats face steeper climbs elsewhere in 2028. North Carolina: Anita Earls' reelection leaves Republicans with a 5-2 majority. Democrats must win two of three Republican-held seats to flip the court. Ohio: Democrats flipped one seat and held another. Republicans will retain a 5-2 majority; Democrats need all…

33e1d7779a:2ef23bc63f59e76e.title: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is harder than it sounds
33e1d7779a:2ef23bc63f59e76e.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:2ef23bc63f59e76e.summary: Reducing the Medicare eligibility age may strike Democrats as a realistic fallback to passing Medicare for All, but it's an option that would be incredibly difficult to pull off. Why it matters: Even incremental steps to address affordability could have huge price tags and prompt fierce industry opposition. Driving the news: Prominent Democrats have been throwing their support behind lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding children's health coverage and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits to Medicare. Incoming Senate health committee Chairman Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called for the package shortly after the midterms, calling it "an immediate first step to Medicare for All." House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is poised to become speaker in January, suggested on "Face the Nation" this weekend that Democrats may be able to work with Republicans on a package after President Trump said he may be open to working with Democrats. Prominent Democrats in both the House and Senate have signed on to legislation that would lower the eligibility age to 50, though the bills are significantly different. The big picture: Democrats' sweeping electoral gains have prompted weeks of discussion about what exactly a push to lower health care costs should look like. The party is united in its desire to roll back the Medicaid funding cuts in last year's tax and spending law and to reinstate enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired late last year — lofty goals for any Congress. There's widespread recognition that Medicare for All won't become law, and that Democrats aren't of one mind on a single-payer plan, with plenty of moderate members still loath to abolish private health insurance. That tension has led to questions about alternatives, and whether "Medicare for More" could be an answer. Between the lines: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would require a series of tough decisions. Just shaving a few years off the current eligibility…

33e1d7779a:1cc1246e11e86ada.title: Nvidia's one-man board: How Trump inherited Jensen Huang's scandal
33e1d7779a:1cc1246e11e86ada.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:1cc1246e11e86ada.summary: A euphoric Wall Street erupted Monday as President Trump personally secured Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, trading on the end of a scandal that — in reality — has only just begun. Why it matters: By assuring Nvidia's board that Huang poses no national security risk, Trump has staked the credibility of the U.S. government on a CEO who lied about his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. It's among the most extraordinary presidential interventions in corporate history — a de facto bailout of the AI industry that will be scrutinized, in excruciating detail, by a hawkish and hostile Congress. Zoom in: Six days after Nvidia's chairman publicly ruled out Huang's return, the board unanimously reinstated him after a secretive White House operation that blindsided even the company's top executives. Trump joined Sunday's board meeting by phone, with one source telling Axios that the president pushed harder for Huang's reinstatement than Huang himself. Nvidia acknowledged relying on assurances from "senior levels" of the U.S. government, even as its own investigation into the suspected Chinese espionage operation remained unfinished. The market reaction was staggering: Nasdaq 100 futures surged to their 7% overnight trading limit, following a brutal week that had raised fears of a broader collapse in AI stocks. Nvidia shares rocketed nearly 31%, adding hundreds of billions to the company's market value and helping Wall Street recover more than half of last week's losses. Trump took a victory lap in an hour-long, freewheeling CNBC interview , declaring Huang "exonerated" and claiming the board ultimately "decided to do what we wanted them to do." Screenshot via Truth Social Between the lines: In orchestrating Huang's comeback, Trump drew on instincts that have defined own tumultuous political career — starting with his conviction that presidential power has "no limits." Never surrender: Trump, the master of the political comeback, appears to see a fellow survivor in…

33e1d7779a:647ad8c89d7d1e35.title: Scoop: Thanksgiving air travel expected to hit 16-year high
33e1d7779a:647ad8c89d7d1e35.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:647ad8c89d7d1e35.summary: Data: FAA; Note: The numbers cover the Monday before Thanksgiving through the Tuesday after. The data includes flights tracked by air traffic control under instrument flight rules.; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Thanksgiving week air travel is expected to reach a 16-year high, with 417,775 flights forecast over the nine-day holiday period from Nov. 23 through Dec. 1, according to FAA figures obtained by Axios. Why it matters: The surge comes on the heels of a historic ground stop that disrupted flights nationwide this month and put a spotlight on potential outages in the nation's aging air traffic control system, which the the FAA is working to modernize. The Thanksgiving rush will be a major test of the Trump administration's push to improve the system's reliability and minimize flight delays and cancellations. By the numbers: The FAA is projecting a 2.2% increase in flights over Thanksgiving week last year and a 7.5% increase over pre-pandemic levels in 2019. Tuesday is expected to be the busiest day, with more than 52,000 flights. Behind the scenes: A newly assembled team tasked with improving the air traffic control system's reliability has been meeting daily for the past week, a White House official said. The FAA is exploring ways to remove vulnerable components from the system and bolster its monitoring capability to detect and quickly address any technical problems before they cause widespread disruptions. The agency also is monitoring potential stormy weather that could disrupt holiday travel, particularly in the East and Midwest. What they're saying: "From standing up a 'Tiger Team' to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we've taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told Axios. "The American people can rest assured we will continue to work around the clock 24/7 to get families where they need to…

33e1d7779a:8e7d30f2ee9bab5e.title: Mississippi's election fights didn't end with Scott Colom's historic Senate win
33e1d7779a:8e7d30f2ee9bab5e.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:8e7d30f2ee9bab5e.summary: Mississippi is facing two fights over its election rules after Democrat Scott Colom 's historic Senate victory: one over voters marked inactive and another over deadlines for receiving mail-in ballots . Why it matters: The disputes could affect how easily eligible voters cast ballots and which mail ballots count when Mississippi elects a new governor and other statewide leaders next year. Driving the news: The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus demanded an investigation Thursday into whether the state's use of credit-reporting data to verify voters' addresses led election officials to incorrectly mark voters as inactive. Lawmakers want to examine the credit-reporting data contracts, instructions sent to county officials and how many eligible voters were incorrectly marked inactive. In one case, a Hinds County voter learned she'd been marked inactive when she arrived at her usual polling place, according to Angela Grayson, director of civic engagement and voting rights at the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable. Her vote ultimately counted, Grayson said. The caucus acknowledged it doesn't know how many voters were flagged in error. Advocacy groups are seeking records to find out. What they're saying: "Nothing has changed fundamentally here in Mississippi," Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, tells Axios. "The laws are still the laws. The governor is still the governor. The state legislature is still overwhelmingly Republican," he said. "It's also plainly obvious that the playbook of reducing turnout, culling the active voter rolls, that's not going to stop." By the numbers: More than 230,000 voters were listed as inactive before the 2026 midterms, up from roughly 171,000 in 2024, according to the Associated Press . Mississippi recorded 21,484 affidavit ballots, the state's version of provisional ballots, this year. That's nearly identical to the 21,321 cast in 2024's presidential…

33e1d7779a:3d02e8891425a932.title: "Troubling and problematic": Gov. Moore rips Trump's Nvidia actions on "The Axios Show"
33e1d7779a:3d02e8891425a932.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:3d02e8891425a932.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore criticized President Trump's involvement in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang , calling it "troubling and problematic" in an interview for "The Axios Show." Why it matters: Moore, chair of the National Governors Association and often seen as a 2028 presidential contender, is one of the most outspoken state leaders pushing for stronger federal oversight of AI companies — but not like this. Driving the news: Trump told CNBC Monday that he spoke directly to Nvidia's board about Huang's return. Trump had previously pushed for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to become Nvidia's leader, but changed tune over the last few days to favor Huang. What they're saying: "The president is not a board member of Nvidia. So, why he is involved in board dealings, I have no idea. ... It seems like it's rules for me, but not for thee," Moore told Axios' Mike Allen in an interview just minutes after the news broke. "You have the wealthy and the powerful and the well-connected that are now making decisions to reinstate, where, frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard." Zoom in: Moore said the "market is being inflated essentially by seven companies," including Nvidia. Huang's return — which led to a stock surge — "highlights how problematic this entire thing is," Moore said. "We are talking about not just millionaires, but billionaires, who are sitting in a quiet room by themselves, making this decision because they know this company is that important." Subscribe to "The Axios Show" on YouTube to watch the full interview with Moore when it's available.

33e1d7779a:4ab2d002625bf9b0.title: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia sparks bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill
33e1d7779a:4ab2d002625bf9b0.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:4ab2d002625bf9b0.summary: Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO is drawing criticism and scrutiny — including about national security risks — from members of Congress in both parties. Why it matters: President Trump's push to reinstate Huang creates a headache for Republicans and new fodder for Democrats eager to deploy their investigative powers when they take control in January. "No national security risk? Based on what," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked in a social media post following the news. "Last week, the board said it didn't intend to reinstate him. I'd like to know what changed," Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said in a statement to Axios. "The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who's been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know," Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) posted on X . Driving the news: The House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees have announced that Huang would testify next week. His reinstatement "changes nothing," an Intelligence Committee spokesperson told Axios on Monday. "When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts." The spokesperson added: "There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee's commitment to oversight." Huang is scheduled to appear before the Senate banking panel on Dec. 3. What we're watching: Top Democrats say they will open their own investigations into Huang's reinstatement when they take power next year. "Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said. "Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump…

33e1d7779a:3f18993f1432d4ea.title: "Too big to fail": The economic fear behind Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback
33e1d7779a:3f18993f1432d4ea.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:3f18993f1432d4ea.summary: President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was " too big to fail " for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios. Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position. Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios. Huang resigned amid allegations he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and subordinates. The stock market's slump prompted President Trump and allies within the administration to push for his reinstatement. "The President was pushing harder than Jensen," one source said. Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting Sunday night to argue for Huang's reinstatement, he told CNBC. Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders. A Trump adviser said allies sought to convince Trump that "deep staters" were working against Huang. The intelligence included findings about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated to senior officials in a memo earlier this year. A Rubio ally said the secretary of state was "mortified" when the memo leaked with his name attached. Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips. Despite the intelligence, Huang remained close to the president while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's inaction fueled tensions between him, Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and others. A senior administration official argued the intelligence never established Huang was compromised,…

33e1d7779a:a2822e4d8e59fe0f.title: Trump presses pause on Army's Iowa lead detonation
33e1d7779a:a2822e4d8e59fe0f.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:a2822e4d8e59fe0f.summary: President Trump ordered the Army to pause plans to detonate unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant, saying the blast cannot proceed without approval from an appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand . The big picture: State officials said last week they only recently learned of the plan to detonate tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, sparking frustration about a perceived lack of transparency from federal officials. The Army, which had delayed the detonation until Wednesday, advised people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors and clean surfaces once the branch declares the airborne exposure risk over. But the threat also sparked warnings in neighboring Illinois, with the American Lung Association saying that residents of eastern Iowa and western Illinois could be exposed to lead. Driving the news: Trump warned Monday that he would hold Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction" if the governor-elect refuses to approve the detonation. " If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation," he wrote in a pointed Monday Truth Social post . State of play: The Middletown, Iowa, blast was initially set for Friday, then delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday. In a Friday letter to Gov. Kim Reynolds, regional EPA administrator Jim Macy said the Army had documented recrystallization of the lead azide, raising the risk of an accidental explosion. The lead azide "is now so sensitive to temperature, friction and shock that it cannot be safely moved, opened, or treated without a significant risk of explosion," per an administration court filing . Friction point: Earthjustice sued last week to halt the detonation on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa…

33e1d7779a:48ab4f104b810ab1.title: Schumer puts Nvidia, Trump on notice after Huang reinstatement
33e1d7779a:48ab4f104b810ab1.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:48ab4f104b810ab1.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) warned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that Congress is coming for answers — whether he's back at the top of the company or not. Why it matters: The embattled CEO's return to the board came as a shock to investors but sent Nvidia's stock through the roof . Now, some lawmakers are warning that his return raises national security concerns. What they're saying: "The Trump Administration's rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Schumer wrote Monday on X. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he's learned nothing from his resounding election defeat. Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain." "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Nvidia and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. Driving the news: Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement as CEO, president and a member of the board Monday morning, less than two weeks after his resignation. Despite saying last week that it did not intend to bring him back, the board did so anyway, amid urging from the Trump administration. Shortly after the announcement, Trump praised the board's decision, calling it "correct and proper," and saying "[t]he Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." Catch up quick: The whirlwind saga around the chipmaking behemoth was sparked by Huang's admitted relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a multibillion-dollar Nvidia…

33e1d7779a:b06266b2f8c3e7a3.title: A red bra, an Nvidia flag and Trump's iconic rally pose: "Sex sells"
33e1d7779a:b06266b2f8c3e7a3.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:b06266b2f8c3e7a3.summary: President Trump posted a doctored image of newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, posing as Trump after his viral assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024. The post came shortly after the embattled Huang was reinstated Monday. Why it matters: The post highlights just how much the White House views Huang as an ally and how the president appears to see Huang's fall from grace and comeback as similar to his own history-making return, despite warnings about national security risks. Driving the news: Nvidia's board reinstated Huang early Monday, declaring him the right person to lead the company. After the announcement, Nvidia shares surged more than 30% by midday, lifting the broader stock market. The reinstatement followed reported pressure from the Trump administration and prompted accountability experts to question the board's judgment . What Nvidia's saying: "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO," Trump wrote in a separate Truth Social post Monday. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security," Trump wrote. Catch up quick: Huang was ousted after he admitted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, who allegedly used her relationship with Huang to help funnel Nvidia chips to China. Reports also alleged he had affairs with at least two subordinates. What Trump's…

33e1d7779a:078cab4f34b367af.title: Doctors who disagree with AI could face legal jeopardy
33e1d7779a:078cab4f34b367af.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:078cab4f34b367af.summary: AI could put doctors who disagree with it in greater jeopardy of losing a malpractice suit, according to researchers who have tested some legal scenarios with mock juries. Why it matters: The public may still be wary about how AI is used in a hospital or doctor's office, but there's also a baked-in assumption that it's never wrong. That can put physicians in a bind when they disagree with an algorithm that flags an abnormality. Some may opt to order costly, possibly unneeded tests if they think it reduces their legal liability. Driving the news: Researchers are using simulated malpractice cases to examine how much AI influences the perception of whether a doctor exercised "duty of care" in treating a patient. The implications are significant: AI systems are used extensively to analyze medical images and improve the accuracy of diagnoses, and demand for tests is rising. But the systems invariably make mistakes. Experts say there are few established legal precedents for how AI might change the nature of malpractice liability in a field like radiology. Physicians are demanding more protections. The American Medical Association this month called for new federal and state legislation that shields clinicians from liability when AI products harm patients. What they found: In a series of simulated court cases, researchers discovered that mock juries were more likely to side with the plaintiff in a malpractice suit when AI disagrees with a radiologist than when AI agrees with them. One scenario involved a brain bleed on a CT scan that resulted in irreversible brain damage. When AI disagreed with the radiologist by flagging the condition when the radiologist didn't think there was one, the jurors sided with the plaintiff more often (72.9% of the time). A second case was built around a missed lung cancer on a CT scan that resulted in the patient's death. When AI was at odds with the physician by saying the patient had lung cancer when the doctor didn't think so, participants…

33e1d7779a:4a35ae62a525f28a.title: UN climate meltdown raises new doubts about talks
33e1d7779a:4a35ae62a525f28a.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:4a35ae62a525f28a.summary: The collapse of UN climate talks without an overarching deal is deepening doubts about the effectiveness of these summits — and bringing fresh calls for a shakeup. Why it matters: Warming is on pace to far exceed the Paris Agreement target of holding long-term temperature rise under 2°C above preindustrial levels — and the more ambitious 1.5°C goal has slipped away . 🏃 Catch up quick: The COP31 talks in Turkey ended Sunday without a high-level "cover decision" of wide-angle agreements and goals. Vulnerable island nations and the EU, among others, objected to a draft deal after some oil-producing countries blocked explicit endorsement of moving away from fossil fuels. ⚔️ Friction point: There was also pushback against proposed text that endorsed carbon capture as a major climate solution. Finance discussions also disappointed advocates, with climate think tank E3G noting that "little or no new and additional money reached the table." 🏀 State of play: Sunday's events reinforce criticisms that the decades-old summit process — which birthed the 2015 Paris deal — is not suitable for spurring policies that meet the scope of the problem. It could add urgency to years-long efforts to revamp how they work. "I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here," Simon Stiell, the top UN climate official, said as the talks closed, per Reuters. 🥊 Reality check: Ending the practice that decisions require consensus — which effectively gives veto power to individual countries and blocs — would be a steep uphill climb. Yes, but: There was some progress at COP31, per groups that track the granular talks. For example, the climate group E3G cites procedural advances on the "Just Transition Work Programme," an initiative created in 2022 to support workers and communities in the energy transition. And dozens of countries endorsed a pledge to bring…

33e1d7779a:670c3d494be5a100.title: DNC limits 2028 primary candidates' ties to big-money groups
33e1d7779a:670c3d494be5a100.author: Holly Otterbein
33e1d7779a:670c3d494be5a100.summary: Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin is moving to restrict candidates' ties to super PACs and dark-money groups in the party's 2028 presidential primary, a shift that could shake up the race for the White House. Why it matters: Most likely Democratic candidates for president were expected to rely on super PACs to boost their messaging — and go after other contenders. The DNC's new rules could complicate their plans and set up a clash between the party chair and soon-to-launch campaigns. Martin's plan will be a real-time test of whether party-driven campaign finance restrictions can function in a presidential primary that will follow a midterm election driven by billions in spending by PACs and dark-money groups. Zoom in: Under the rules that the DNC is announcing Monday, Democratic presidential candidates must disavow any super PACs or dark-money groups that either back them or attack their opponents in ads. If presidential hopefuls don't follow the guidelines, the DNC warns, they won't be allowed on the stage at primary debates. A DNC official said the change is backed by progressives such as Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), as well as more moderate Democrats such as Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison. For years, the party's left wing has pushed for party primaries to ban super PACs and dark-money organizations, a term for 501(c)(4) groups that aren't required to disclose their donors. Yes, but: It's not clear whether the DNC's shift will be substantive — or merely symbolic. Super PACs, which can raise unlimited amounts of money, already are barred by law from directly coordinating with candidates. Even so, such groups often work alongside candidates while remaining technically separate. The DNC rules stipulate that candidates must sign a pledge to disavow such funders. Super PACs could, however, continue to spend on behalf of candidates that distance themselves from them. In practice, though,…

33e1d7779a:873d35bb929db2a0.title: Trump's top intelligence official is also taking charge of cyber policy
33e1d7779a:873d35bb929db2a0.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:873d35bb929db2a0.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity. Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure. Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director. Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed. Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy. What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios. "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate." The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks. The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks. Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's…

33e1d7779a:e604e64dcce13e80.title: How bitter rivals Buttigieg and Klobuchar went from enemies to friends
33e1d7779a:e604e64dcce13e80.author: Alex Thompson
33e1d7779a:e604e64dcce13e80.summary: To the surprise of many Democrats and even some of their former aides, Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar now consider themselves friends after their bitter clashes during their campaigns for president in 2020. Their journey from snarky tension to "real respect and friendship," as Klobuchar describes it, is a story of how two ambitious Democrats came to appreciate each other once the heat of a presidential primary had subsided. Why it matters: It's also a reflection of how Buttigieg — who's weighing another run for president — has become a well-regarded Democratic stalwart after many in the party viewed him as a presumptuous lightweight when he ran six years ago as a little-known 37-year-old former mayor of South Bend, Ind. "I'm sincerely grateful for Amy's friendship," Buttigieg, who was President Biden's transportation secretary, told Axios. "My appreciation has continually grown for her substantive leadership and sense of humor alike." "I know there are people that run against each other for president and literally hate each other," Klobuchar, who's in her fourth term in the Senate but will leave in January to become Minnesota's governor, told Axios. "That was far from the case for us." Flashback: A casual observer might see that as a bit of revisionist history. The Buttigieg-Klobuchar spats during the 2020 Democratic primary were some of the most vicious of that campaign. Aides from both sides can still quote the barbs, word for word. "I wish everyone was as perfect as you, Pete," Klobuchar sniped at one debate in Las Vegas before saying "You've memorized a bunch of talking points and a bunch of things." She added after the debate that Buttigieg was "haughty" and that "given the guy [Trump] we have in the White House, maybe you need someone who's a little more humble." Buttigieg repeatedly mocked Klobuchar for not remembering the name of the president of Mexico in an interview. He said Klobuchar was "not able to speak to literally the first thing about the…

33e1d7779a:7759c31f23259b81.title: Scoop: DeSantis' secret book project fuels 2028 speculation
33e1d7779a:7759c31f23259b81.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:7759c31f23259b81.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is quietly working on a book, two sources tell Axios — a project likely to fuel speculation about his making another run for the White House. Why it matters: DeSantis hasn't publicly acknowledged the book project or disclosed what it will be about. But writing a book is often the first step toward a presidential campaign, and it could give the term-limited governor a platform to lay out his vision for the Republican Party's future. DeSantis' state was a rare bright spot for Republicans in this month's midterms, as Democrats made historic gains across the nation. Driving the news: Word of DeSantis' book comes as he's become increasingly outspoken on a range of policy issues, particularly the economic and social impact of artificial intelligence — potentially offering clues about what the book might address. DeSantis has become a vocal critic of the potential dangers of AI, warning that it could eliminate jobs, threaten children's safety and privacy, and drive up electricity bills as data centers expand. DeSantis has pushed for an "AI Bill of Rights" and signed state legislation aimed at preventing tech companies from passing the costs of data centers on to residential consumers. His stance has put him at odds with the Trump administration's efforts to limit states' ability to regulate AI. DeSantis has emphasized affordability, immigration and education — issues likely to remain central to national politics long after he leaves office. Zoom out: DeSantis has made other moves that could keep him in the national spotlight after he leaves office in January. NBC News recently reported that DeSantis is preparing to launch a conservative think tank, which could enable him to retain a political and donor infrastructure. After the midterms, DeSantis embarked on a flurry of media appearances that resembled a victory tour, highlighting how Florida Republicans had largely escaped the Democratic wave. Yes, but: Some DeSantis allies are highly skeptical…

33e1d7779a:ef8996ba043db33e.title: Scoop: The Pentagon's case for Canada to "get serious" on defense
