33e1d7779a:ef8996ba043db33e.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:ef8996ba043db33e.summary: The Pentagon accused Canada of failing to become a "credible partner" due to its faltering military readiness and low defense spending, according to a sharply worded fact sheet issued by the Pentagon to justify new restrictions on America's northern neighbor. Why it matters: The restrictions deepen tensions between the U.S. and Canada over trade and defense, as Ottawa reconsiders billions of dollars in purchases of American weapons. The new restraints — which do not affect defense or intelligence sharing— limit U.S. military personnel from fraternizing with their Canadian counterparts at official events without prior authorization from the Pentagon, an official told Axios. The Pentagon fact sheet has not been reported. But the Washington Post first reported the restrictions, followed by the New York Times . Zoom in: At the heart of the dispute are NATO defense spending goals and military readiness under the bilateral North American Aerospace Defense Command where, the memo says, Canada falls short in three ways: 🛩️ Air: Only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet "was serviceable from 2025-2026, largely due to ageing equipment and personnel shortages," the Pentagon fact sheet says. The shortfall limits Canada's "ability to meaningfully contribute to air defense commitments … to defend our North American airspace against all threats." Canada relies on the U.S. and NATO for airborne early-warning aircraft but is negotiating to buy its own from Sweden's Saab. ⚓️ Sea: Just 53.9% of Canada's naval fleet was "serviceable" from 2025-2026, limiting its "ability to monitor maritime approaches to North America," the fact sheet says. Only one of Canada's "four ageing Victoria-class submarines" is "seaworthy at any given time." Canada has a new fleet of conventional submarines, manufactured by ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems, coming on line, but until then, its undersea "capability will be limited." 🪖 Land: The Canadian Army had an operational readiness rate of 48% from…

33e1d7779a:9fffc85d9ad117db.title: Behind the Curtain — AI 2027: The reckoning
33e1d7779a:9fffc85d9ad117db.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:9fffc85d9ad117db.summary: We've talked to more than 50 leaders in government, AI, business and cyber — from let-'er-rip AI accelerationists to shut-'er-down critics — and they were unanimous on one chilling assessment: Cyberattacks on business and critical infrastructure will be constant, increasingly sophisticated and highly disruptive over the next 18 months. These leaders describe 2027 as the year cyber becomes like weather: Outages will be frequent, disruptive, occasionally scary, and something people and companies must learn to navigate and live with daily. The chances of widespread disruption or real damage are rising fast. Why it matters: We write this neither to forecast nor frighten. Rather, we're sharing what government and AI leaders say privately but won't say publicly. The big picture: The disruptions of the past two weeks — from a global Microsoft outage to the FAA grounding air travel to a consumer banking glitch at Chase — were a mild preview of what experts expect is coming. Bridgewater Associates, the world's largest hedge fund , put it bluntly in an assessment this month: "[We] are managing money based on a one-in-three chance of an economically destabilizing attack within the next year." Horacio Rozanski , chairman and CEO of Booz Allen, calls this the "fog before the war" — a foretaste of greater chaos to come, when agentic invaders reach their full potential and can attack "at the speed of thought." "Now is the time to take as many precautions as you can," Rozanski said. "Recognize that this is coming." Most of these malfunctions appear to have resulted from companies and government trying to secure their computer and infrastructure systems against future large-scale cyberattacks. This pattern will persist. Many future ones will be actual cyberattacks, carried out by U.S. rivals or smaller bad actors, using increasingly powerful AI to spot and exploit security vulnerabilities across society and our daily lives. Most top AI and government leaders expect at least…

33e1d7779a:8e31919b700f1ad7.title: Trump says he'd work with Dems to cap credit card interest, fees
33e1d7779a:8e31919b700f1ad7.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:8e31919b700f1ad7.summary: President Trump said Saturday he'd gladly work with Democrats to cap interest and fees on credit cards , arguing that card companies simply make too much money now. Why it matters: Though some argue capping rates would save consumers billions of dollars a year, the banking industry is equally adamant that it would deny credit to millions of Americans by making lending too risky. Driving the news: Trump, in a Fox News interview Saturday morning, was asked whether a rate cap on cards was something on which he could find common ground with Democrats. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), poised to be the new chair of the Senate Banking Committee, is an outspoken advocate for such caps and has recently said she's ready to work with Trump to pass a bill. What they're saying: " I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot — and the credit card fees that they charge. I'm all into it," Trump said . "I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise. But what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said 'let's charge a fee that's too high.' So I'm all for that," Trump said. "The credit card companies, they're getting too much. The fees are too high and the interests are too high." Context: The credit card industry argues that capping interest rates would reduce the revenue needed to cover losses when borrowers default, prompting lenders to reject more applicants. Reality check: This isn't the first time Trump has said he'd cap card rates. In January, he said on Truth Social he'd set a 10% cap for one year and any lender that didn't comply would face legal consequences. Nothing came of the threat, which credit unions claimed could deprive more than 47 million people of access to cards. Nonetheless, the mere idea was enough to send shares in major card issuers lower, and prompt a full-throated response from the industry. What to watch: As much as both Warren and Trump support…

33e1d7779a:36f54bef9a0c6a16.title: Trump says FBI hack might expose Russia "hoax"
33e1d7779a:36f54bef9a0c6a16.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:36f54bef9a0c6a16.summary: President Trump on Saturday said the reported hack of a crucial FBI database might have a silver lining — it could, he claimed, expose more details of what he called the " Russia Russia Russia hoax ." Why it matters: The president remains laser-focused on many of his past grievances about the FBI , even as the public grows increasingly alarmed about the vulnerability of government infrastructure. Driving the news: CNN and NBC reported Friday night that the FBI was looking into an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, which connects local and national law enforcement for information sharing. That follows breaches and outages that struck the FAA, NSA and USDA, just in the last week. What they're saying: Trump was asked about the FBI reports in a Fox News interview Saturday morning. "Well we just heard about it and I will say that it's not good, I don't like that," Trump said. "But maybe we'll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise. You had the Russia Russia Russia hoax, you had all these other hoaxes," he added, referring to Ukraine in particular. "Maybe we'll learn about them. Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place." "I always like to put things in a positive spin," Trump added. "Wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia Russia Russia," he said. The intrigue: The president's comments come just days after a summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia, after which he described Putin as a " friend ." What to watch: It's not clear who breached the FBI database, or what they might do with the data obtained.

33e1d7779a:e962c27d9d8b5b10.title: After historic Southern wins, Black organizers prepare a push for governing power
33e1d7779a:e962c27d9d8b5b10.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:e962c27d9d8b5b10.summary: After years of being overlooked by national Democrats, Black organizers are using stunning Southern election upsets in the pursuit of something more lasting: a new generation of candidates who can win and govern. Why it matters: Activists say the 2026 midterms proved Southern races long dismissed as unwinnable could flip with grassroots organizing and investment. Now they're building a multiracial, working-class political bench — from school boards to statehouses. Organizers want to turn Black political gains into a durable Southern coalition united by economic interests, not just opposition to Republicans. By the numbers: The midterm election results gave organizers fresh ammunition. Roughly nine in 10 Black voters backed Democratic House candidates nationally, according to the AP Voter Poll . Democrats flipped 10 South Carolina House seats, seven won by Black candidates, ending the GOP supermajority, the South Carolina Daily Gazette reports. State of play: The Working Families Party plans candidate recruitment events in Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina and Mississippi in early 2027, targeting community organizers, teachers, young activists and other political outsiders. It plans training, digital outreach and spending to support dozens of Southern candidates. Its Southern Made initiative aims to recruit and train 1,000 working-class candidates by 2030. Zoom in: South Carolina illustrates the opportunity. WFP-backed Jumelle Brooks , a home health care provider, lost a 2024 House race by roughly 700 votes before winning this year by nearly 10 percentage points. Another WFP-backed Democrat, Sonja Ogletree Satani , won a Charleston-area rematch. What they're saying: "We are building concentrated governing power," Britney Whaley, WFP's Southeast regional director, tells Axios. Whaley wants clusters of allies in elected bodies who can pass legislation, not isolated progressives powerless to advance an agenda. "Black people across the country voted for historic…

33e1d7779a:8b96bab42047b10f.title: Second judge to block Trump's contested D.C. arch
33e1d7779a:8b96bab42047b10f.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:8b96bab42047b10f.summary: A second federal judge will block construction on President Trump 's embattled arch set to be erected near Arlington National Cemetery , multiple outlets reported Friday. Why it matters: It represents yet another barrier to the multi-year project to build a 250-foot arch that challengers said would obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema said she will issue preliminary injunction that will indefinitely block the project, which she reportedly called a "rushed job" from the bench Friday. Zoom out: Brinkema's rebuke comes after D.C.-based District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday extended her separate order blocking construction on the arch for two weeks. Chutkan, who is overseeing consolidated challenges from military veterans and from the District of Columbia and Virginia, issued her initial temporary restraining order earlier this month. That order prohibited construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery reported. What they're saying: "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. State of play: The legal hurdles came after the National Capital Planning Commission , which is stacked with Trump loyalists, gave its final approval for the project. Challengers, however, have argued the project requires congressional approval — and as Chutkan noted , "Congress has not enacted any statute authorizing construction of the Arch." Between the lines: The arch is one prime example of the president's quest to remake the nation's capital as he sees fit, from a…

33e1d7779a:0569dbb41fdaad66.title: Congress gets a historic overhaul from every direction
33e1d7779a:0569dbb41fdaad66.author: Kathleen Hunter
33e1d7779a:0569dbb41fdaad66.summary: Senate data includes members who served nonconsecutive terms; House data does not. Data: House historian, U.S. Senate ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Americans want change , and they're about to get it: A perfect storm of congressional retirements, primary upsets, gerrymandering, flipped seats and lawmakers who died in office has created the biggest freshman class in decades. Why it matters : Congress had a 14% approval rating (not a typo) when Gallup polled registered voters in October. That's its lowest pre-midterm number since 1974. The big picture: The Senate is on track for its biggest freshman class since 1946. In the House, it's shaping up to be the biggest since 1992. Zoom in: The turnover featured data points that would be stunning on their own, let alone together. 28 House lawmakers chose to run for their next elected office outside the House, Pew noted in September. Six lawmakers died in office this Congress, the most in nearly 20 years. Thirteen House and Senate incumbents lost primary races. The bottom line: Congress is saying goodbye to former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). They've been in Congress since 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987, respectively.

33e1d7779a:1de069dddb7de2a5.title: Trump floats major tax on U.S. companies constructing data centers overseas
33e1d7779a:1de069dddb7de2a5.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:1de069dddb7de2a5.summary: President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do. Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint , as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose. What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials. "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country. Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes. He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities. "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it." Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes. Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally. Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried : Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country. Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S. "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday. Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence." Go deeper: Voters deliver "AI…

33e1d7779a:2f78c477f8b8bcd8.title: Johnson urges Republicans to show up to work
33e1d7779a:2f78c477f8b8bcd8.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:2f78c477f8b8bcd8.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren't over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. Why it matters: Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP's legislative agenda. GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation. Eleven of those 14 won't be returning next Congress. Driving the news: "To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote in a Friday letter to his colleagues . "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," he added. Zoom in: The outgoing speaker pointed to government funding, the annual defense authorization bill and permitting reform as priorities for the final weeks of the Republican majority. He also said he wants to pass "every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes" and force Democrats to take politically difficult votes. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson wrote.

33e1d7779a:e1b8db06b8a485ad.title: Trump secretary's Christian messages to staff went "too far," judge rules
33e1d7779a:e1b8db06b8a485ad.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e1b8db06b8a485ad.summary: A federal judge said Thursday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' overtly Christian messages to department employees went "too far" and put enough pressure on staff to raise a First Amendment violation. The big picture: The Supreme Court has repeatedly weighed the boundaries of the Establishment Clause . While the judge said Rollins could express her religious beliefs with interested colleagues, she concluded the department-wide messages overstepped those boundaries by amounting to coercion. But a USDA spokesperson slammed the decision as "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" in a statement to Axios. Catch up quick: The complaint from a federal employees union and individual staffers alleged Rollins sent "increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including an Easter email where she celebrated "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind." The USDA employees who sued, who came from varied religious — and nonreligious — backgrounds, reported that the messages made them feel pressured to share Rollins' beliefs. What's inside: District Judge Trina Thompson ordered Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when disseminating messages which convey religious content." She determined the messages overstepped and suggested "acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." "After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion," Thompson wrote. She said she was not trying to regulate Rollins' own religiosity; rather, she directed Rollins to follow her own department memorandum on religious expression rights, which states employees can't "use official authority to pressure subordinates." The other side: The administration argued that the employees lacked jurisdiction and that the…

33e1d7779a:3eaddc5cb54edcc5.title: Anthropic is public, now comes the hard part
33e1d7779a:3eaddc5cb54edcc5.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:3eaddc5cb54edcc5.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios With its IPO done and dusted, Anthropic's shareholders will be watching its progress toward becoming a business that doesn't need constant capital infusions from investors and vendors. Why it matters: Anthropic — along with OpenAI — is at the heart of the industry that's dominated the equity and debt markets for the last four years. Much of the AI infrastructure boom is ultimately aimed at supplying computing power to these two companies. Yes, but: The bill for that data center investment will start to come due over the next few years. And Anthropic and OpenAI are going to have to pay for quite a bit of it. How it works: Anthropic has covered much of its computing costs thus far by selling parts of itself off to compute vendors like Amazon and Alphabet, and by raising more cash from other investors. But eventually the company's core business will have to generate enough money to cover those costs on its own. Case in point: Anthropic's filings say it is on the hook for roughly $900 billion in spending commitments — mostly for data centers and computing power — with about half of that due before the end of 2030. After the IPO, Anthropic is expected to have roughly $200 billion in cash and short-term investments in the bank, which should buy it some time. But its sales will have to be a lot higher to just cover computing obligations, let alone the profits ANT's new shareholders are expecting. By the numbers: As the chart above shows, Anthropic posted a loss of roughly $23 billion on revenue of nearly $17 billion in the third quarter. It's true that much of that loss stems from a non-cash accounting charge of almost $22 billion. But even the more favorable metric of operating income — which strips out the paper losses and gains that can obscure the company's core earnings power — still shows an operating loss of more than half a billion dollars in the third quarter. The bottom line: Anthropic still has a long way to go before…

33e1d7779a:d84b36548cf39d0a.title: GTA VI hijacks America
33e1d7779a:d84b36548cf39d0a.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:d84b36548cf39d0a.summary: The internet's warring tribes converged Thursday for the loud, lawless debut of " Grand Theft Auto VI ," as 13 years of anticipation culminated in one of the great viral spectacles of all time. Why it matters: In a media landscape splintered into dozens of distinct realities, the GTA launch gave Americans a rare common obsession — refracted through vastly different platforms, personalities and worldviews. By Thursday night, GTA VI had generated an estimated $2.36 billion in sales from nearly 25 million copies — almost triple the first-day revenue of its record-breaking predecessor in 2013, according to Sensor Tower . The irony is rich: Amid political rancor and mounting technological anxiety, millions of people sought refuge in a virtual America gone gloriously, spectacularly off the rails. Zoom in: GTA VI drops players into Vice City, a fictionalized Miami that serves as a sprawling digital fever dream of violence, celebrity, corruption and distinctly American absurdity. Players can rob banks, steal planes, wrestle alligators and wreak havoc — or pass the afternoon fishing, shopping, working out and tending to the relationship between the game's central characters. The astonishingly detailed world teems with influencers, conspiracy theorists, criminals and social-media parodies, offering limitless opportunities for the outrageous encounters now flooding the internet. Zoom out: GTA's return has revived decades-old arguments about whether violent video games encourage real-world aggression, while igniting a far stranger debate over masculinity. On Fox News , commentators warned that the game's carjackings and shootouts could desensitize young players to crime. One contributor likened giving children the game to handing them a gun. Meanwhile, corners of the online "manosphere" expressed outrage over missions that reward players for buying flowers, running errands and showing affection toward their girlfriends. Between the lines: GTA VI was an internet phenomenon…

33e1d7779a:9b0b3e4964905173.title: America's religious "nones" move from voters to lawmakers
33e1d7779a:9b0b3e4964905173.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:9b0b3e4964905173.summary: America's religious "nones" have gained a visible foothold in Congress: Five lawmakers will claim no religious affiliation in January, up from a single member just two years ago. Why it matters: Washington remains far more religious than the nation it represents. But the last two election cycles have put a series of cracks in that political glass ceiling. By the numbers: Religiously unaffiliated voters made up 27% of the 2026 midterm electorate, up from 23% in 2024, according to preliminary Fox News voter polling . Just three of 532 lawmakers surveyed at the start of the 119th Congress claimed no religious affiliation, according to Pew Research Center . Pew counted one additional humanist. All three lawmakers who claimed no affiliation — Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Abraham Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Emily Randall (D-Wash.) — won reelection in November. State of play: They'll be joined in January by Democratic Reps.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Fred Wellman of Missouri — who publicly acknowledged their nonreligious identities before winning their Nov. 3 elections. Rabb, a five-term state lawmaker representing a majority-Black Philadelphia district, won the seat of retiring Democratic Rep. Dwight Evans. Wellman, a retired Army officer, ousted seven-term Republican Rep. Ann Wagner in suburban St. Louis, flipping a longtime GOP stronghold. Their wins mark a breakthrough for congressional candidates who openly embraced their nonreligious identities before Election Day, according to Secular Coalition for America. Zoom in: Rabb thanked atheists for supporting his campaign after winning his May Democratic primary. Wellman defeated Wagner roughly 51% to 46%, according to Ballotpedia . His pitch? Affordability, corruption and accountability — not his lack of faith. Zoom out: The nonreligious political bench stretches well beyond Capitol Hill. More than 100 openly nonreligious lawmakers are expected to serve in at least 38 state legislatures, up from 81 in 33 states,…

33e1d7779a:8ab9901e455dca05.title: Medicaid expansion isn't a "slam dunk" for new Dem governors
33e1d7779a:8ab9901e455dca05.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:8ab9901e455dca05.summary: Democrats' sweeping electoral wins jump-started prospects for Medicaid expansion in red and purple states that rejected full expansions of the program under the Affordable Care Act. But budget realities could make newly elected Democratic governors pump the brakes. Why it matters: The changing of the guard sets up a test of whether states can expand coverage to more low-income residents right after Republicans in Congress weakened financial incentives for doing so. States that are facing serious budget shortfalls and daunting cost projections already are signaling they may defer until conditions are more favorable. State of play: Incoming Democratic governors in Wisconsin, Georgia, Texas and Kansas who campaigned on Medicaid expansion are now in a position to expand health coverage, and have more Democrats in their legislatures to help. Wisconsin Democrats have arguably the most leverage now that they've captured the state Senate and Assembly in addition to keeping control of the governor's office. Plus, the state already covers adults with incomes up to the federal poverty level. Expansion advocates in Georgia and Texas face a heavier lift, with Republicans still controlling at least one legislative chamber. And in Kansas, the GOP lost its supermajority in the House, a key obstacle in past Medicaid expansion fights, but still controls both chambers. Between the lines: Each state faces unique considerations. But one thing is true for all of the holdouts: The incentives for expanding aren't what they used to be. Though the federal government still would pay for 90% of the expansion cost, last year's GOP reconciliation law made major policy changes and cuts to the program. Expansion states now face stricter limits on provider taxes used to finance Medicaid, as well as on extra payments they make to hospitals and other providers to go beyond standard Medicaid rates. They've also lost an important bonus: A temporary 5% increase in federal assistance for newly…

33e1d7779a:a4600d27a831a904.title: Phoenix mayor walks fine line on AI boom
33e1d7779a:a4600d27a831a904.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:a4600d27a831a904.summary: Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego wants more tech investment in her city — but on her terms, as data centers strain resources and frustrate residents. Why it matters: Phoenix has become a bellwether for the AI industry's growing demands on electricity and water in an increasingly hot, resource-constrained world. As the mayor, Gallego is navigating an outsized dilemma facing communities nationwide: How to embrace the AI boom while protecting residents and resources in an increasingly hot world. "I do want us to lead in technology, and I want us to be a tech-forward community," Gallego said at a recent event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios. But she added: "I want companies who care about our community and will give back to it, and not just a race to see who can get the deepest incentives and the cheapest" power. "We're open for business, but we're not for sale," she said. Zoom out: Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies in her efforts to strike the balance she wants. Democrats flipped both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs won reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966. Affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate, Gallego said. Catch up fast: Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity. Now the debate is expanding from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. State of play: Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, has spent recent years trying to balance that. She helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions. The state enacted a three-year pause on new applications this summer. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium, favoring more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes.…

33e1d7779a:9340b1ea7fd25225.title: Senate passes Trump-backed permitting bill
33e1d7779a:9340b1ea7fd25225.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:9340b1ea7fd25225.summary: The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill Thursday night that's designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects. Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan, which has White House support, would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. Driving the news: The vote was 62-33. The bill would still have to pass the House before the end of the year, and any differences would have to be worked out by both chambers before President Trump could sign it into law. Catch up quick: It would make significant changes to federal permitting, including: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. Language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once they're issued, a priority for renewables groups and Democrats upset with Trump administration barriers. State of play: There are also provisions to ensure that data centers pay for needed grid upgrades, and expand federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects. Friction point: Many environmental advocates argue that the bill would dangerously erode safeguards in the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. Multiple tribal groups still oppose it despite changes aimed at easing concerns about consultation on historic preservation. Energy and business groups, ranging from renewables developers to manufacturers to the oil and gas industry, are lobbying for the measure. The AFL-CIO and many individual unions back it, too. What's next:…

33e1d7779a:e354279c70d7cf84.title: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
33e1d7779a:e354279c70d7cf84.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:e354279c70d7cf84.summary: On his way back from China Thursday aboard Air Force One, President Trump called in to a meeting his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding in Berlin with a group of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this," Trump said, according to people in the room. Why it matters: Instead of turning his historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin into a modern-day Yalta Conference, as some European and Ukrainian officials feared , Trump tried to use it to propel his push for peace in Europe. Driving the news: Trump met Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen. Their meeting wasn't originally on the schedule, but Trump wanted to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine directly with the Russian president, a U.S. official said. "Who is he? He's my friend," Trump said when he entered the meeting room where Putin was waiting. Later in the day, Witkoff and Kushner told European leaders in Berlin that Trump pressed Putin to move on the peace talks, telling the Russian leader that now is the time to get a deal, according to a European official. Trump also asked Xi for his help in ending the war during their bilateral meeting. "He sent a very strong message to both of them [Putin and Xi] on the desire for peace, and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said at a press conference on Thursday. Behind the scenes: As Trump wrapped up his meetings in China and headed back to Washington, his envoys started their talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Zelensky and other European leaders. Kushner and Witkoff tried to reassure the group that Trump doesn't intend to cut a deal with Putin over their heads. "President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to…

33e1d7779a:003d5d2199be5280.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:003d5d2199be5280.summary: House Republicans chose fighter Jim Jordan over the more experienced Steve Scalise to lead them after taking a midterms beatdown. Now they're facing a similar choice over who should lead them on House Oversight. Why it matters: Whoever gets the top Republican spot on the Oversight Committee will be the first line of defense on some of the most deeply personal issues for President Trump and his inner circle. A pair of Texas House Republicans, freshman Rep. Brandon Gill, 32, and three-term Rep. Pat Fallon, 58, want the job that could make them a national star, or leave them taking the heat if Democrats land damaging revelations. Driving the news: Democrats are preparing a barrage of investigations , putting Trump's family, finances and closest advisers in their crosshairs. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is running to chair House Oversight next year, sent a dozen letters Wednesday targeting figures including Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance. Democratic allies want a plan "to compel disclosure and testimony," according to a Tuesday letter — led by Public Citizen and Indivisible — that was signed by 103 groups and obtained by Axios. The White House is pushing back on Hill Democrats, with its top lawyer warning that some Democratic investigative tactics could cross into criminality. Zoom in: Gill has made a name for himself with fiery committee confrontations and viral moments. He's also proven to be a prolific fundraiser. "Gill is the next Jim Jordan," a source close to Jordan told Axios. "He practices, he's smart." Fallon has served on Oversight since arriving in Congress in 2021. He previously chaired Oversight's subcommittee on economic growth, energy policy and regulatory affairs. "I've built great relationships and a clear resume of rigorous, result-oriented oversight that reflects what the committee has achieved on behalf of the American people," Fallon told the Texas Tribune in September. Between the lines: Gill's lack of…

33e1d7779a:71ae0620b8fefc17.title: House Democrats recoil at forcing December shutdown to cut Iran war funding
33e1d7779a:71ae0620b8fefc17.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:71ae0620b8fefc17.summary: House Democrats are largely steering clear of threats to shut the government down in December if Republicans put forward legislation that maintains funding for the war in Iran. Why it matters: Much of the party's left flank — including some members of Congress — think it's a fight they need to pick after their midterm landslide. "The American people were loud and clear on November 3rd: they want an immediate end to Donald Trump's reckless war in Iran," Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in a joint statement on Wednesday. The pair said they will "oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran" because it would "defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end—now." State of play: The Democrats' majority doesn't officially begin until Jan. 3, while federal funding is set to run out on Dec. 11. Republican leaders are struggling to pass party-line procedural votes and will probably bring up their funding patch under a fast-track process that requires bills to pass with a two-thirds majority. In other words: The GOP will almost certainly need a large number of Democratic votes to pass any funding bill, especially if some of their own members defect. What they're saying: "Whatever they have to do to get it through they should do it, but I hope there's not a shutdown," said Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the outgoing chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition. "I don't think we should shut down the government, we take that way too casually as it is, so I'd be leaning into not doing it," said Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.). Said Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio): "Everyone should do whatever they can to avoid a shutdown. The impact it has on the economy, but workers in particular, it's just not fair." Between the lines: Even some progressives acknowledged their imminent House majority takes a lot of the pressure off the December fiscal deadline. "If I can defund [the war] in…

33e1d7779a:4393151b5d6a6b70.title: Exclusive: Rep. Gregory Meeks vows to reclaim Congress' powers from Trump
33e1d7779a:4393151b5d6a6b70.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:4393151b5d6a6b70.summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said Thursday Congress is going to reclaim powers long ceded to the executive branch at the Axios Future of Defense summit. Why it matters: As the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Meeks is putting the Trump administration on notice that it's foreign policy decisions are going to be challenged through legislation and oversight hearings. What they're saying: "Whether it's a Democratic president or Republican president, we've ceded too much and we've got to stand up and take it back," Meeks told Axios' Colin Demarest. "We do, at times, have to make some difficult decisions, and not just punt them away to the executive branch, because when you do that, it's hard to get them back." Meeks also suggested that incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) may be willing to take the Trump administration to court if needed to enforce congressional oversight. "If it takes some litigation to do that, we will do that," Meeks said. "Speaker Johnson wouldn't do it. I think Speaker Jeffries will do it." Catch up quick: Meeks will likely become Foreign Affairs committee chair in January, riding the blue wave that gave Democrats the ability to control Congress' legislative agenda. Zoom in: Meeks didn't rule out calling Secretary of State Marco Rubio to testify before the committee. "The jurisdiction of the House Foreign Affairs Committee is the State Department," Meeks said. Later, he added more broadly, "[y]ou can run, but you can't hide... We're going to use the power that the committee and the Constitution gives us to make sure that we're calling in members of that administration, so they have to answer to the American people, why what has taken place has taken place." Zoom out: Meeks has already sent document-preservation letters to seven agencies, including the State Department, USAID and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, warning them to avoid destroying records that could be relevant to oversight efforts.…

ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.author: Van Reenen, John
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

ecbefe1924:db363258cf9b18bd.title: TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale
ecbefe1924:db363258cf9b18bd.author: Diyi Yang
ecbefe1924:db363258cf9b18bd.summary: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O*NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65%of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O*NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. Relative to the task data from the O*NET 31.0 database for the sampled occupations, TaskNet covers 75% of the 118 published O*NET tasks and adds 79 tasks with no O*NET counterpart and 58 that refine existing statements. It covers 89% of tasks reported by held-out workers, compared with 79% for O*NET, and a larger share of the activities described in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%). Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated. Because such estimates guide…

ecbefe1924:4cc4d8be07d9455a.title: The Dynamics of Rent-Sharing across Occupations
ecbefe1924:4cc4d8be07d9455a.author: , Matteo
ecbefe1924:4cc4d8be07d9455a.summary: We study how firm-level productivity gains are shared across the occupational hierarchy. Using Portuguese matched employer-employee data linked to firm balance sheets (2004–2019), we develop an algorithm that identifies permanent shocks to firm value added and estimate occupation-specific rent-sharing elasticities in an event-study design. Pass-through declines steeply along the job ladder: the elasticity of pay premia to value added per worker is about 0.20 for managers and supervisors, 0.11 for qualified workers, and 0.06 for low-qualified workers. This gap has widened over time, increasing within-firm inequality, as pass-through to low-qualified workers has halved. This decline is consistent with de-unionization, while we show that minimum wage increases do not crowd out rent sharing at the bottom. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.author: Xu, Yaling
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.author: Asani Sarkar
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

b3ea4f41ab:62365c5d1c14bedd.title: From Single to Multi-Project Participation: SME Absorptive Capacity in Horizon 2020
b3ea4f41ab:62365c5d1c14bedd.author: Loreta Isaraj
b3ea4f41ab:62365c5d1c14bedd.summary: This paper presents an analysis of SME participation in the European Framework Programme for Research and Innovation (Horizon 2020), focusing on the role of firm age in shaping funding engagement and success. Our dataset comprises a broad sample of Italian SMEs, allowing us to distinguish between firms participating in a single project and those engaging in multiple projects. We find it important to distinguish two patterns of participation: single engagement, where firms participate only once throughout the entire seven-year duration of Horizon 2020, and sustained involvement, where firms secure funding for multiple projects over time. Our econometric results indicate that older SMEs, benefiting from accumulated experience and established networks, tend to perform better in multi-project participation, achieving higher funding efficiency compared to younger SMEs. In contrast, younger SMEs, while more agile and innovative, often face challenges in sustaining long-term engagement due to resource constraints and limited administrative capacity. These findings underscore the importance of firm age as a key determinant of absorptive capacity and funding success in EU research programs, with implications for policies aimed at improving SME access to international R&D funding.

b3ea4f41ab:345df8f627e6476e.title: The Start-up Venture Capital Innovation System Comparison with industrially financed R&D projects system
b3ea4f41ab:345df8f627e6476e.author: Angelo Bonomi
b3ea4f41ab:345df8f627e6476e.summary: This paper concerns a study on the start-up venture capital (SVC) system, now becoming an important structure for generation of new technologies. SVC system may be considered an evolution of R&D projects system financed by industrial capitals. The study considers start-ups companies of technological nature characterized by carrying out not only R&D but also searching business models suitable for the developed technology. Venture capital (VC) owns the more radical aspect of the SVC system, looking for selling the developed technology or business, and refinancing new start-ups instead of exploiting the use of the technology as done by industrial capital financing R&D projects. The SVC system have the objective to reach an exit selling the developed technology or business and obtaining an adequate return of investment (ROI) for the VC. The SVC system operates in a financing and refinancing cycle that may reach an equilibrium when obtained ROI covers costs of both successful and abandoned start-ups and cost and rewards of VC. Should ROI be higher than the equilibrium value it might start an autocatalytic process generating a high number of technologies and ROI. The SVC cycle may be simulated mathematically showing that a selection strategy of financed start-ups based on high potential ROI and team validity gives in practice superior economic results in respect to a selection strategy based on the probability of a successful exit of the start-up. Comparison of SVC system and industrially financed R&D projects shows that the SVC system is superior in the development of radical technologies with suitable business models in respect to industrially financed R&D projects that are limited by pre-existent strategies in firms financing R&D.

b3ea4f41ab:8c221db68127ce93.title: Business Models of AI-driven Sustainability Startups: A Taxonomy
b3ea4f41ab:8c221db68127ce93.author: Beck, Joshua
b3ea4f41ab:8c221db68127ce93.summary: Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and sustainability efforts are fostering innovative business models that integrate both domains. This paper develops a taxonomy to classify business models for AI-driven sustainability startups. Following the methodological approach of Nickerson et al. (2013), a taxonomy comprising of 43 characteristics across nine dimensions was developed through five iterations utilizing the Business Model Canvas as a foundational framework. This taxonomy was developed and validated by analyzing 90 European startups, resulting in the categorization and clustering of five types of business models. By establishing a common vocabulary, this research addresses fragmentation and creates a foundation for comparative research and theory building in the intersection of AI and sustainability. The final taxonomy provides a tool for evaluation, classification and communication of business model types for both researchers and stakeholders, while remaining adaptable of future extensions and specifications to reflect innovation and evolution of AI-driven sustainability startups.

b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.title: Productivity review of the Netherlands: Supporting business dynamism to revive productivity growth
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.author: OECD
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.summary: The Netherlands has one of the highest levels of labour productivity in the OECD, but growth has slowed over the past decade. The slowdown partly mirrors global trends but has been accentuated by weak investment and declining business dynamism. Against this background, this paper provides a cross-country comparative analysis of the role of firm entry, exit, growth and resource reallocation across firms, in shaping recent Dutch productivity performance. A set of policy simulations suggests that, even though the country performs well on a wide range of policy indicators, some reforms could boost business creation and job reallocation, thereby lifting productivity. The most promising measures include streamlining labour legislation, upgrading education and training, reducing the administrative burden on start-ups, refining the insolvency regime and further encouraging R&D and venture capital investment.

b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.title: Transforming Textile Waste into Circular Value: Innovation, Community Participation and Sustainable Entrepreneurship in Micro and Small Enterprises
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.author: Sweta Patnaik
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.summary: In an era marked by economic uncertainty and environmental urgency, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning to sustainable innovation as a pathway to resilience and growth. This paper examines how the transformation of textile off-cut waste into functional and marketable products serves as both an entrepreneurial response to material scarcity and a strategic contribution to the circular economy. In contrast to high-capital technological innovation, this form of resource-based creativity offers accessible, low-cost solutions for emerging enterprises, particularly in the fashion and textile sectors. Drawing on examples of micro and small businesses navigating uncertain economic terrain, the study highlights how such innovations can generate value, reduce waste, and meet growing consumer demand for sustainability. While many entrepreneurs falter in the face of early challenges, those who reframe problems as opportunities particularly through material reuse are better positioned to survive and scale. This paper argues that innovation rooted in environmental consciousness and adaptability is not only viable during times of uncertainty but essential for long-term entrepreneurial success and inclusive economic recovery.

b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.title: Current state and development prospects of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan: From an emerging market to a systemic driver of economic growth
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.author: Malika Azimova
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.summary: This article examines the institutional and economic conditions shaping the development of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Drawing on an analy-sis of the legal and regulatory framework, industry statistics, field research, and comparisons with selected international markets, the study identifies the main fac-tors limiting the sector's growth and proposes a phased model for its institutional development. Particular attention is given to regional disparities, the sectoral composition of the market, and the potential of locally developed franchise sys-tems to support entrepreneurship and expand employment opportunities. The empirical evidence covers the period 2024?2025 and includes an analysis of commercial concession agreements as well as expert interviews with market par-ticipants from eight regions of Uzbekistan.

b3ea4f41ab:da2b93eef72d9b34.title: Schumpeter and Samuelson Revisited: Sweden’s Capitalist Reversal and the Post-2008 Mixed Economy
b3ea4f41ab:da2b93eef72d9b34.author: Jakobsson, Ulf
b3ea4f41ab:da2b93eef72d9b34.summary: This paper revisits Schumpeter’s prediction that capitalism’s success would ultimately undermine its social and political foundations. We first reassess Sweden, where postwar policies favored large corporations, concentrated ownership, weakened entrepreneurship, and culminated in the radical wage-earner fund proposal. Sweden then reversed course: deregulation, tax reform, financial liberalization, and stronger private ownership helped generate a dense entrepreneurial ecosystem and Europe’s most vibrant listed-company sector. The Swedish case therefore refutes deterministic accounts of capitalism’s decline while showing how institutions can accelerate or reverse the tendencies Schumpeter identified. We then examine Paul Samuelson’s reformulation, which emphasized the political consequences of economic stagnation, inequality, and perceived unfairness in mixed economies. His forecast fitted the 1980s and 1990s poorly but has become more relevant since the 2008 financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, heightened geopolitical conflict, and the intensified rivalry with China. The emerging outcome is still not socialism, but a more politicized mixed economy in which private enterprise remains economically essential yet politically contested.

b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.title: Heterogeneous Firms, Growth and the Long Shadows of Business Cycles
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.author: Adam Hal Spencer
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.summary: Do ï¬ rms differ in their innovation response to business cycles? What economic forces shape this heterogeneity? And does it matter for aggregate propagation? We document substantial heterogeneity in ï¬ rm-level R&D cyclicality, develop a theory to explain this fact, and validate its key mechanism in the data. In a tractable model of business cycles and innovation-driven growth, endogenous selection makes R&D particularly responsive to aggregate conditions for ï¬ rms close to the exit margin. Consistent with this mechanism, ï¬ rms closer to exit display more procyclical R&D in the data. Quantitatively, selection and endogenous growth interact powerfully: selection generates heterogeneous R&D cyclicality, while endogenous growth translates these heterogeneous responses into persistent aggregate effects. Ignoring heterogeneous R&D cyclicality misses roughly half of the long-run output cost of a severe recession.

b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.title: Women Artisans in Economic and Social Development: A Systematic Literature Review on Entrepreneurship, Cultural Heritage, and Empowerment
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.author: Yingying Zhang Zhang
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.summary: Introduction: Women artisans play a crucial role at the intersection of cultural heritage, entrepreneurship, and rural development, acting as preservers of age-old traditions and catalysts for community economic growth, although the scientific literature on this phenomenon remains fragmented. Objective: To synthesize and analyze existing evidence regarding women artisans, focusing on their roles as agents of economic development, preservers of cultural heritage, and drivers of social empowerment initiatives. Method: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA methodology, involving searches in the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Following a screening process, 30 studies were analyzed using both bibliometric and hermeneutic approaches. Results: Systemic barriers-such as limited access to finance and sociocultural restrictions-were identified alongside effective facilitators, such as cooperatives that generate income growth. Conclusions: Women's artisan entrepreneurship constitutes an integrated model of sustainable development that links personal empowerment, cultural preservation, and economic growth. Women artisans act as agents of social transformation, creating impacts that extend beyond their own lives to benefit entire communities.

b3ea4f41ab:704543d164d86b98.title: The Emperor has no Clothes: A Critique of the Knowledge Spillover “Theory” of Entrepreneurship
b3ea4f41ab:704543d164d86b98.author: Wim Naudé
b3ea4f41ab:704543d164d86b98.summary: The knowledge spillover theory of entrepreneurship (KSTE) claims that new ventures commercialize knowledge that incumbent firms leave unexploited, thereby linking entrepreneurship to economic growth. This paper studies the mathematical basis and empirical tests for the KSTE as provided in Acs et al. (2009). It is shown that the knowledge filter is absent; that entrepreneurial labour is idle; that the aggregation of individual start-up hazards is invalid; that the knowledge-filter interaction required by H2 is not established, while H3’s negative entry response is conditional on an inconsistently stated interpretation of the institutional parameter; and that the valuation condition is dimensionally inconsistent. Its empirical design further relies on a pooled correlation between R&D intensity and the knowledge stock that does not establish their within-country relationship, and on inference that does not account adequately for country-level dependence. The subsequent model of Acs and Sanders (2013) does not solve the central problem: by assuming that all ideas spill over, it removes the knowledge filter altogether. It is concluded that the KSTE is a promising narrative, not a theory..

b3ea4f41ab:e0159f2f4f9b1327.title: Migrant entrepreneurship, high-growth firms and cities
b3ea4f41ab:e0159f2f4f9b1327.author: Sivropoulos Valero, Anna
b3ea4f41ab:e0159f2f4f9b1327.summary: High-growth firms represent a small share of businesses in OECD countries, but disproportionately drive national economic activity. This paper examines migrants' role in founding high-growth firms, and the urban nature of high-growth entrepreneurship. Using novel founder- and company-level data on over 12, 000 UK companies and 15, 000 founders, we analyse the characteristics of migrant founders and the firms that they build. We establish six new facts. First, relative to the UK migrant population, migrant entrepreneurs are substantially over-represented among founders of high-growth potential firms. Second, compared to UKborn founders, migrant founders are positively selected on human capital, but negatively selected on entrepreneurial experience. Third, high-growth potential firms are highly urbanised, and those with a migrant (co-)founder display a distinctive urban geography. Fourth, firms with mixed native-migrant founding teams show faster employment and revenue growth than all-UK teams. All-migrant teams show weaker growth premia. Fifth, compared with UK-born founded firms, firms with mixed native-migrant founding teams have more distinctive strategic positioning, with fewer peers. Sixth, for co-founded firms, our results vary by birth countries, first language and urban location. Migrant-founded firms in London and conurbations exhibit the largest performance premia.

b3ea4f41ab:45dfc155dc716b40.title: Algorithmic Alertness and Imprinted Exits: Artificial Intelligence, Founder Characteristics, Opportunity Recognition, and Exit in South America
b3ea4f41ab:45dfc155dc716b40.author: Quispe, Sofía
b3ea4f41ab:45dfc155dc716b40.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how new ventures are conceived, built, and ultimately exited, yet most theorizing about these shifts has been developed in North American and European settings where capital markets are deep and institutions comparatively stable. This essay develops a conceptual framework that links founder characteristics, AI-enabled opportunity recognition, and entrepreneurial exit in South America, a region marked by institutional voids, concentrated family ownership, rapid consumer adoption of AI, and thin, contracting equity markets. Drawing on upper echelons and imprinting theories, the cognitive literature on opportunity recognition, and an emerging view of AI as an entrepreneurial actor rather than a passive tool, we argue that AI does not so much substitute for founder characteristics as re-weight them. Algorithmic search lowers the cost of identifying opportunities but raises the premium on founder judgment, entrepreneurial drive, and political skill, which govern whether AI-surfaced opportunities can be legitimized and exploited where formal institutions are weak. At the exit stage, founder imprints formed under the region's recurrent macroeconomic crises shape not only whether founders sell or list, but whether they later reverse a public listing altogether, a pattern currently visible in the wave of delistings on Brazil's B3. The essay advances six propositions and outlines an agenda for research on AI-augmented entrepreneurship in emerging economies.

18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.title: Anchor or sinker – Large firms, anchoring capacity and regional development
18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.author: Nilsson, Magnus
18d1edb9f2:ce90462aa69c2379.summary: This paper ties together two literatures which explain regional anchoring from different perspectives. One is based on the role of large organizations in anchoring an industry in a region, the other is systemic and deals with anchoring processes that circulate and embed knowledge. Each leaves implicit what the other explains. The aim is to understand how anchor effects and regional anchoring capacity interact across different regional contexts. Illustrative cases from three Swedish regions show how the two both diverge from and reinforce each other, anchor without anchoring and anchoring without an anchor, depending on regional configuration and anchor control.

18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.title: University as catalyst of public R&D expenditures? An empirical assessment on EU NUTS 3 regions
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.author: Saverio Barabuffi
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.summary: This study examines whether universities shape the regional innovation effects of public R&D expenditure and whether this role varies across regional development trajectories. We analyse a panel of 1166 EU NUTS 3 regions over the period 2007-2020, combining data on European public R&D funding, patenting performance, university presence and regional development traps. Toa ddress the endogeneity of public R&D expenditure, we employ a control function aproach. The results show that public r&D expendirue positively affects patenting performance in both university and non-university, but the difference between them is not statistically significant. University presence therefore does not sistematically amplify the returns to public R&D. However, its moderating role becomes more pronounced in regions exposed to development trap risk and in regions experiencing persistent stagnation, while evidence is weaker for trap intensity. These fundings suggest that universities act as contingent rather than unviersal catalyst of public R&D. Their contribution appears particularly relevant in vulnerable and persistently stagnant regional trajectories, but less able to offset sever structural constraints. The study contributes to debates on the geography of public R&D and regional development traps by showing that the effectiveness of research funding depends not only on institutional presence, bu also on the development rajectory in which that institutional capacity is embedded.

18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.title: Place-based multi-system innovation: the case of the twin transition technologies in European regions
18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.author: Ron Boschma
18d1edb9f2:c83ad7175e77dfed.summary: There is increasing interest in studying how multi-system innovation (MSI) emerge across regions. Understanding it requires attention to the co-evolutionary dynamics among systems and to their spatial co-location. Integrating insights from the Sustainability Transition and Evolutionary Economic Geography literatures, a framework is proposed to study the critical emergence of innovation at the intersection of digital and green technologies, as outlined in the European twin transition agenda. Despite numerous studies, it remains unclear how specific components and capabilities recombine within regions to support the emergence of twin technologies. This framework is explored empirically in a study of 271 European NUTS-2 regions, using a random forest classification model to identify which configurations of regional technological trajectories most strongly support the emergence of twin technologies during the period 2000-2021. Using patent data, the results show that digital and green follow different trajectories into twin regional specialisation. Digital technologies contribute primarily through relatedness among themselves, while green technologies contribute when co-located with digital ones, with Artificial Intelligence being the most consistent interaction. These findings inform place-based regional innovation strategies by showing that the emergence of twin technologies depends not only on the accumulation of digital and green knowledge bases, but also on the specific configurations through which regions enter the twin technological space.

18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.author: Juan Cruz Lopez Del Valle
18d1edb9f2:43e63914665bf0ef.summary: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily. Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation. Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them. Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts. Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin’s ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.

18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.title: From research & innovation to deployment - Tapping into the R&I policy potential to transform knowledge into products
18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.author: Igor CZERMAINSKI DE OLIVEIRA
18d1edb9f2:539ee550d8e511a5.summary: This paper analyses how EU Research & Innovation policy can support the transition from knowledge generation to deployment and industrial scaling in strategic technologies. It uses RADAR, a policy simulation model, to test what emergence-oriented and industrial-scaling oriented policies can most effectively foster the translation of R&I outcomes into products that can successfully be commercialised and adopted. Results suggest that these two policy logics affect different outcomes and operate on different timelines. Early emergence support is especially relevant for product development outcomes, while scaling support becomes more important for installed capacity, employment and market capture once an upstream base exists. The results should be read as exploratory scenario evidence rather than as forecasts or optimal policy prescriptions. Their policy value lies in clarifying bottlenecks, sequencing issues and monitoring needs across different technology domains.
